inline.s: Instructions to Zhou Yangru

Zhouzi asked for instruction on the essential purport of the Dharma-characteristics teaching. The Elder therefore brought up the Sixth Patriarch’s verse on consciousness and wisdom: “The great perfect mirror wisdom is pure in nature; the wisdom of equality has no sickness in the mind; the wisdom of marvelous observation sees without effort; the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done is like a round mirror. The five and eight, the six and seven, turn from effect and cause; but only the names are turned — there is no real nature. If at the place of turning one does not linger in feeling, then amid teeming activity one forever dwells in nāga samādhi.” In these eight lines he exhausts the heart’s marrow of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and lays bare the very root of nature and characteristics. Yet those who count jewels and tally sand, greedy for much and unable to chew what they bite off, generally look on this as idle furniture; there is never one who truly fixes his eye on it. How pitiable! Everyone says the Sixth Patriarch could not read and had no understanding of the teachings — how then could he speak thus? They do not realize that the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ wisdom-life is wholly contained, with nothing left over, in eight words: “The three realms are mind only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only.” Because they are mind only, the three realms are still, utterly without a single thing. Because they are consciousness only, the ten thousand dharmas are manifold — for the ten thousand dharmas are nothing but transformations of consciousness only, and when sought in one’s own mind and nature they are utterly unobtainable. Therefore the Buddhas and Patriarchs taught people only to say: outside the mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable. This is precisely what Huangmei revealed at midnight: “From the first, not a single thing exists.” In this one phrase all Buddhas of the ten directions and three times, and the Patriarchs of every generation, are packed so tightly that it cannot be broken apart. Hence the robe and bowl were entrusted with it. And the two schools and five houses all unfolded from this one phrase. Where was there ever a division into nature and characteristics? Now, looking at the verse on consciousness and wisdom, let me break it open a little. If we take it that the three realms are mind only, there is no place to begin speaking. It is because this mind is deluded that it turns into consciousness, and so loses the name of true suchness and is called only ālaya-consciousness, also named storehouse consciousness. This consciousness is the whole of true suchness transformed; it is precisely what is meant by “the conditioned and the unconditioned joined together to form it.” It is the root of the real and the deluded, of delusion and awakening; the basis of birth-and-death and of ordinary beings and sages. The Laṅkāvatāra says: “The ocean of storehouse consciousness is forever still; it is moved by the wind of objective conditions. Great waves surge through the dark abyss, and there is no time of ceasing.” Since it says the storehouse consciousness is the ālaya, and yet also says it is forever still, then it is fundamentally unmoved. What is moved is not the storehouse consciousness but only the wind of objective conditions. The verse says: “If the objective conditions before are not, the mind too is not.” So then what grasps at objects is not the storehouse consciousness but the mind of birth-and-death. This mind of birth-and-death is provisionally named the seventh consciousness, but in truth it is the stirring thought of the eighth consciousness — what is called the vital impulse. Once this impulse is stilled, the objects before one are suddenly empty, and though the sixth consciousness may still discriminate, it has nothing to lodge upon. As for the first five consciousnesses, they have no substance of their own; they are merely the storehouse consciousness functioning in response to conditions. They can illumine objects but cannot discriminate, and so it is said they are “like a round mirror.” What discriminates the five sense objects is not the five consciousnesses but the consciousness of mind that arises at the same moment; therefore it is said to have accomplishment. If discrimination does not arise, then seeing is without effort. Seen thus, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally real, and so it is called “pure in nature.” Its fault lies in a single thought of giving rise to mind, and this is the sickness of the mind. Where there is arising there is ceasing. This arising and ceasing is like the flowing of water: there is no flow apart from water. It is only because of water’s nature of not abiding that a mark of flowing is seen; and where there is flowing, it is clear that it is not the still water of a deep pool. Hence the Laṅkāvatāra speaks of two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing: the arising-abiding-ceasing of marks, and the arising-abiding-ceasing of the surging stream. Both belong to the storehouse consciousness. If arising-and-ceasing is not extinguished, the first seven consciousnesses arise; if arising-and-ceasing is extinguished, only the one pure reality remains, and the nature of true suchness is thereby restored. Restored, consciousness is no longer called consciousness but wisdom; hence “no sickness in the mind.” What the Sixth Patriarch’s verse sets forth is the turning of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms. The great perfect mirror wisdom is what the storehouse consciousness turns into; the wisdom of equality, what the seventh turns into; the wisdom of marvelous observation, what the sixth turns into; the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, what the first five turn into. Because delusion belongs to the functioning of the storehouse consciousness, the real is likewise likened to a round mirror. But the sixth and seventh are turned first, in the midst of cause, while the five and eight, being one substance, are perfected only at the fruit. Seen thus, consciousness is fundamentally unreal, yet delusion has these two functions. Therefore it is said: “only the names are turned” — the name is changed but not the substance. Moreover this substance does not lie in meditation or cultivation, but only in all the affairs of daily use; sages and ordinary beings turn it at the same moment, and everything depends on whether one lingers in feeling or not. Hence the difference between sage and ordinary being, between delusion and awakening. Zhouzi, if you have set your mind on this, then earnestly fix your eye on the place of turning in daily use, and try to settle it for yourself.
Instructions to Shu Bosun

The scholar Shu Bosun had his mind set on the Way and asked for instruction. I therefore taught him, saying: Laozi said, “In pursuit of learning one daily increases; in pursuit of the Way one daily decreases. Decrease and again decrease, until one arrives at non-doing.” Students increase their knowledge and views and take this as progress; they do not realize that as knowledge and views increase, the view of self prevails. When the view of self prevails, the temper grows more arrogant; when the temper grows more arrogant, the feelings grow more reckless; when the feelings are reckless, desire blazes and the nature is dimmed. When the nature is dimmed, the Way recedes further. Therefore one who pursues the Way takes decrease as increase. Our nature is fundamentally pure, utterly without a single thing — this is what is meant by “the substance of the nature in which not the finest dust is established.” But because habitual defilement is thick, it issues as greed, hatred, delusion, and pride; and so one indulges feeling and material desire. The thicker material desire becomes, the more the nature is daily dimmed — this is what is meant by “the harm of having a surplus.” One who pursues the Way today should only decrease his surplus in order to restore what the nature lacks. If the substance of the nature is complete, the light of the Way daily shines. Issuing from it, one becomes loyal, filial, benevolent, and righteous; extending it, one governs the state and the family, and its benefit is widespread and its virtue great. To attain merit and fame that do not decay — all this is the gain of decrease. Hence in the hexagrams of the Changes, decreasing the upper to benefit the lower is called Increase, and decreasing the lower to benefit the upper is called Decrease. If one does not know what to decrease, and merely takes the increase of knowledge and views as learning, then increase and decrease are inverted; how could one then fully realize one’s nature? Therefore one whose will is set on the Way values decrease.
Instructions to Wen Zhen

Confucius said: “If wealth could be sought, even as a whip-holding groom I would do it. If it cannot be sought, I will follow what I love.” He also said: “Wealth and honor gained by unrighteousness are to me as drifting clouds.” Now if wealth could be sought, he would not be ashamed to hold the whip; yet having said it could be sought, he also said wealth and honor are as drifting clouds. Did he seek it, or did he not seek it? What he means is: wealth and honor that are unrighteous are like drifting clouds — a strong statement that they must not be sought. This is the teaching by which the gentleman endures poverty, and the reproach by which the petty man runs to excess. Our sage taught people this as the foundation for settling their destiny and steadying their will. Alas, alas! People today do not understand the foundation of the great destiny, but stand trembling in the field of success and failure; they have not understood the source of nature and life, but harbor thoughts of gain and loss. When gain and loss alarm the mind, taking and rejecting go divergent ways, and flying thoughts crisscross in the breast. To seek a settled will and clear principle, renewed virtue and advancing practice — can it be had?
Instructions to Liu Pingzi

It is not hard to turn toward the Way; what is hard is to give rise to the resolve. It is not hard to study the Way; what is hard is to seek outside. It is not hard to understand the Way; what is hard is to pick and choose. It is not hard to enter the Way; what is hard is to be content with oneself. It is not hard to awaken to the Way; what is hard is to seek the wondrous. A student of the Way who sees through each of these and is not deceived by others has a broad mind and a glad spirit, and walks alone, free and unconstrained — such a one is called a person of wondrous penetration.

“Natures are near to one another; habits carry them far apart.” These words point directly to the shortcut of cultivation through a thousand ages. If we only knew that our own nature is near, and that it is only through habit that it becomes distant, we would at once cut off the vital pass: inner habit would not be allowed out, outer habit would not be allowed in. With both ends cut off, what lies between is naturally alone. In that aloneness, this is precisely what is meant by “as though something were standing there, towering.” If one arrives at the ground where that towering thing alone remains, then the nature restores itself.

Ziyu said: “The way of learning and inquiry is nothing else than seeking back the mind that has strayed.” And yet there are those whose minds never cease seeking, and whose learning and inquiry remain unclear. Why? The fault lies in “releasing without releasing” and “seeking without seeking” — a vague, shadowy semblance that they regard as of no importance. If one knows what it is to release without releasing, then one is naturally not released; if one seeks without seeking, that is true seeking. Master Ziyu, who saw the nature and understood the mind, had nothing more than this in his single transmission and direct pointing. If you have the will to turn toward the Way, take this as your standard.

The Way lies in daily use, yet people do not know it; the Way is right before the eyes, yet people do not see it. Knowing daily use but not knowing the Way, seeing what is before the eyes but not seeing the Way — it is not that the Way is far from people; people themselves are far from it. Hence it is said: the Way is before the eyes, yet it is not what is before the eyes; the Dharma is likewise not apart from what is before the eyes, yet it is not reached by ear or eye. If you can pass through what is before the eyes — at the passes of favorable and adverse, in the realm of praise and blame — and are not ensnared, but stride straight through with your whole body, then with such an attitude the sage is not confined to the three dynasties, and past and present do not depart from a single thought. If you have the will to turn toward the Way, then from the first arousal of the resolve, enter right here.
Instructions to Ou Jiafan

The world takes the loyal minister and the filial son as the highest principle, and says that loyalty springs from filial piety and begins in serving one’s parents. The saying goes: “In thinking of serving one’s parents, one cannot but know others; in thinking of knowing others, one cannot but know Heaven.” Now Heaven is simply our own innate heavenly nature. In this world a person may feign almost anything, but the thought of serving one’s parents is the truest of all, because it comes forth from the heavenly nature. We who have received this nature and become human — if we do not know the original suchness of the heavenly nature, we do not know what is truly precious in being human. If one can truly know what is precious in being human, then toward all vain, mixed, defiled, and turbid affairs one will naturally not dare let them lodge in the breast and obscure the originally possessed emptiness and clarity. Once the original clarity is restored, the sage and worthy are within oneself. Hence it is said, “The Way is not far from man” — this is what it means.
Instructions to Li Zijin

Human nature is fundamentally clear, but is dimmed and covered by material desire and the dust of feeling; hence people do not know it in daily use. Therefore it is said, “Natures are near; habits carry them far apart.” If we have the will to work at restoring the nature, there is no need to seek outside; we need only take the places in daily seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing where habitual defilement and material desire weigh heaviest, and moment by moment overcome and remove them. When this overcoming has gone on a long time, things dissolve and dust vanishes, and the original clarity reveals itself of itself. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is clean, the brightness appears. Yet the substance of the mirror was originally bright; it does not await polishing to have it. Whoever has the will to work at the Way should take the overcoming and polishing of bad habits as the first ground of entry.
Instructions to Li Zirong

The ancients said: “When cutting hair, one should reach the skin; when trimming nails, one should come to the flesh” — meaning that it must be done thoroughly. Therefore a student of the Way must first establish a long-range, unretreating resolve, and apply a solid, earnest, painful effort. It is like climbing a mountain ten thousand fathoms high: one does not stop until one reaches the very summit. Step by step exert yourself; thought after thought do not retreat. Do not be swayed by praise or blame, shaken or robbed by right and wrong, or crushed by hardship and obstruction. Be like one person fighting ten thousand. If you falter even a little, all your previous work is lost. How then could one reach the state of unretreating peace and joy without a firm and solid mind?
Instructions to Ou Jiake

It is said: “There is no one who does not eat and drink, yet few can know the flavor.” This says that the Way lies in daily use, very close at hand, yet those who know it are rare. The ancients said that apart from putting on clothes and eating food there is no other matter. So then, within past and present, those deceived by clothes and food are many. One who is not deceived by them may be called a hero. A student of the Way need not seek the wondrous elsewhere; if in all the conditions of daily use he is not deceived, and with one glance sees through the place of putting on clothes and eating food, that is true work that reaches upward. One who has his will set on the Way should do it amid daily use.
Instructions to Liang Tengxiao

When a gentleman lives in the world and has not yet met his opportunity, there is none who does not vow to assist his ruler, shelter the people, and establish an undecaying enterprise. But once he enters the registry of office, he sets his heart only on making a name, forgetting what it was that made for true merit. In time he is gradually stained by the customs of the age; his mind and spirit grow turbid, and before he knows it he has drifted onto the road of wealth and honor. In the extreme he no longer even scruples about his reputation, and his original resolve can no longer be found. Why? Because his first vow did not come from the fundamental reality, but was merely a vain admiration and a deluded thought. Since it was never a firm and unshakable resolve, how could it establish an undecaying enterprise? Master Liang Tengxiao is firm-boned and free in spirit — by no means a man of the dust of the world. Whenever he followed me, there was no word or phrase he heard that did not stir his heart to vigilance. Once he asked for instruction, and I told him: a student should indeed set his will on the Way and virtue; and whoever sets his will on the Way and virtue must first investigate our fundamental reality, and let it flow from the true nature. This true nature is vast beyond measure, bright and pure, swept utterly clean of the finest dust. This is the substance of our nature — what is called benevolence. Within this substance not a speck of dust is established; but if there is a single deluded thought, that already belongs to self. With self, one stands opposed to things; once thing and self are divided, self and other are set up; once self and other are set up, the substance of the great unity is blocked and dulled, and cannot be benevolence. When the original substance is blocked and dulled, all delusions arise; even if one has the will for merit and fame, it is all discharged from deluded thought, and whatever one does is not real. Since the root is deluded, one’s footing is unsteady; and so, once one enters worldly conditions, it is only fitting that one is at once stained by vulgar custom. From today, Master Liang, you should work at your own nature and investigate from reality. If you cannot yet thoroughly investigate the root of your own nature, then simply take the Sixth Patriarch’s saying — “not thinking of good, not thinking of evil; at that very moment, what is the Original Face of the Venerable One?” — as your huatou, keep it in your breast, and day and night earnestly investigate it. Investigate to the place where not a single thought arises; suddenly you will recognize your Original Face, and only then will you see that Old Lu did not deceive me.
Instructions to You Juezhi

The essence of prajñā is complete in everyone; it is only because habits are thick or thin that the obstruction is heavy or light, and so people differ as wise or foolish. Know therefore that when greed, hatred, delusion, and craving are present before you, it is the moment when the whole substance stands fully exposed — only it is turned about by turbid wisdom and is not noticed. This is what is called “daily use without knowing.” Alas! The sage is no different from the ordinary person; it is only that when the conditions before him in daily use are tangled and interwoven, he sees through them at a glance and is not deceived, blinded, or robbed by them. Seen from this, the wisdom of equality is present in every thought; like a great blaze, it makes all conditions transparent of themselves.
Instructions to the Upāsaka Wang Boxuan

The ancients often spoke of people amid the toil of the dust who have their will set upward and seek to escape birth and death — they called this “a lotus growing in fire,” because it is truly rare. For all living beings, through measureless kalpas, have wallowed in the five desires, burned by the fire of affliction, blazing day and night, never once turning the light around to gain a moment of coolness — and so it is even now. If amid the thicket of blazing flames one suddenly turns the head around and at once thinks of a way out, is that not a lotus born within the fire? Boxuan is a man of Min who came to trade in Yue, and came to pay his respects to the Elder and seek the Dharma of liberation. The Elder pitied him, gave him the five precepts, and taught him the method of Buddha-recitation, that he might devote himself single-mindedly to the Pure Land. The scripture says: “When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.” Since our own mind is the Buddha and mind alone is the land, purity and defilement are not two, and mind and Buddha are one suchness. Contemplate thus and think thus; thought after thought permeate and cultivate, and with the single mind pure, light shines forth and reflects, and the lotus Buddha-lands of the ten directions stand bright before you. Why speak only of a lotus born in a house of fire?
Instructions to the Chan Monk Jijue on His Pilgrimage to Putuo

The Chan monk Jijue was about to go east to pay homage at Putuo and begged a word to carry as the weight of his pilgrimage. The Elder instructed him, saying: The ancients left home solely for the great matter of birth and death; hence they traveled with staff in hand, visited and inquired of good teachers, climbing mountains and crossing rivers, and would not stop until they had brought about clear awakening. Those who leave home today bear the name of pilgrimage in vain: this year Wutai and Emei, next year Putuo and Funiu; with every mouth they say they are worshipping famous mountains and rejoicing in the monasteries, but in truth they do not know what a famous mountain is, or what a monastery is for. They do not even know who is a good teacher; they only remember how high and deep the mountains and waters were, and whether the gruel and rice in the monasteries was fine or coarse. They walk the whole world over and have not one word to bring home to their own mountain — is this not pitiable? The southern sea is boundless; it is the swell of the bitter sea of birth and death. The scenery of Mount Putuo is the eternal abiding of the Great One’s dharma-body. The tide resounding in the sea is the Great One’s universal gateway of teaching. If the Chan monk can truly cross the sea of birth and death, then he will behold the Great One at the universal gate and hear the sound of Dharma on the sea cliffs, turning back to hear his own nature — and he need not step outside the gate once. Why must he wait to reach Putuo before seeing? If he cannot, then the long road will be an empty going and an empty coming; even if the Great One appeared at his brow, he could not pull out the root of his birth-and-death karma. Let the Chan monk settle this for himself. And if the Great One has any words, then when you return you should repeat them to the Elder. Be careful not to waste your straw-sandal money in vain.
Instructions to Liang Zhongqian (Jiayin Year)

Liangzi, whose four marks were Zhongqian, had followed the Elder for years. The Elder loved him because his heart was upright and his spirit generous. Whenever he saw an injustice — whether or not it was his business, or wherever righteousness could be done — he would cast aside his body and life to stand in its way. The Elder often reproved him for being rough and flighty: he had the substance of the Way but lacked the work of containing and preserving it. He was like a fine horse without bit or bridle, and in the end could not avoid a fall. When the Elder was about to set out, Zhongqian escorted him to the boat at Shaoyang and asked for a word of Dharma to write on his sash. So the Elder wrote this and sent it to him. I say that Liangzi is a man of the Way: his heart is upright and not crooked — this is the root of the Way. His generosity is close to courage; his rushing to aid the urgent is close to compassion. But to forget his body and go to it is not to weigh his strength, not to examine what is fitting, not to probe the root but to attend to the branches. All this is driven by a rough and flighty temper, not issued from the power of the Way. The sages of old moved through the world with substance and function fully manifest, and so responded without missing the moment, like a bright mirror reflecting beauty and ugliness, like a balance determining weight — very far from recklessly following blood and temper. From now on, Liangzi, you should first wash away your habits and give your mind to the Way. Take the Sixth Patriarch’s huatou, “from the first not a single thing exists,” and lay it across your breast. At every moment watch the place where a thought arises; whether good or evil, give the huatou one thrust, and it perishes on the spot. Dense and unbroken, make this root huatou your own original spirit. When it has long been pure and familiar, mind and objects will naturally be empty and at leisure; in movement and stillness, in speech and action, wherever you meet anything, the huatou will be present before you — that is illumination and function clear and undistracted. Sustained by the power of samādhi, you will of yourself not fall into the realm of the rough and reckless, nor follow the heels of others. Even in reading books and writing essays this root investigation need not be hindered: when you have read and written, put it down and return it to “from the first not a single thing exists.” Then your breast will naturally be even and composed. After a long time you will suddenly see that this mind has no substance at all, as though you were within a treasury of light, and every pore of your body is the work of benefiting beings. What body or life would there then be to cast away? Working thus, containing and nurturing, the essence of mind will be present; reading a book, you will meet the sages’ minds mind to mind; writing an essay, it will flow from your own nature. This is the true accomplishment of a generous and manly person — what is called grasping the pivot at the center of the ring, to respond to the inexhaustible. Then even merit and enterprise will all become undecaying. Since Liangzi has this root, why should he fear and not do it?
Instructions to Liu Zhong’an (Winter of the Guichou Year)

I was staying at Wuyang, and for a time many followed me. I saw Liuzi: firm-boned and whole in spirit. I said that he had long planted the seeds of prajñā and that his vessel was near to the Way. I was about to travel to Nanyue, and Liuzi escorted me to the boat, where he especially asked for instruction, saying: “This disciple’s mind for the Way is most earnest, but because old habits are thick and deluded thoughts entangle him, he cannot escape straight upward. I beg the Master to instruct me.” The Elder said to him: “If you know deluded thought, then deluded thought cannot of itself entangle you. Since it is called deluded thought, it has no substantial reality; like a flower in the sky, how could it bear a fruit in the sky? Because you do not understand that deluded thought is fundamentally nonexistent, you take it as a real thing and set yourself in opposition to it, and thought after thought you wrestle with it, never having a single thought of rest. Thus you make deluded thought the master, and your own original substance is buried by it — that is why you find the Way so hard to reach. Have you not heard how a monk asked the ancient worthy, ‘What does one do when deluded thoughts do not stop?’ The worthy said, ‘Deluded thoughts are not evil.’ The Sixth Patriarch, in the assembly at Huangmei, managed only to say, ‘From the first not a single thing exists.’ From today, when you work, simply take the phrase ‘from the first not a single thing exists’ as your huatou, and day and night earnestly investigate it. Just watch where deluded thoughts arise, and on no account follow them along; give them one thrust on the spot, and they will naturally vanish without trace.”
