Instructions to the Chan Monk Guanzhi Yun

One who studies the Way must first see through all the conditions of the world and not be turned about by deluded conditions. Second, he must rouse a single resolve for the great matter of birth and death, and settle it with an iron-and-stone heart, so that deluded thoughts and clinging conditions cannot seize away his will. Third, he must wash away all the bad habitual perceptions and views from before, leaving not a hair behind. Fourth, he must truly and truly let go of body and life, not allowing sickness, death, or evil conditions to obstruct him. Fifth, he must give rise to right faith and right view, and must not listen to the errors of false teachers. Sixth, he must recognize the place where the ancients applied their minds earnestly, and take it as his huatou for investigation. Seventh, in all places of daily use right mindfulness must be present before him, not deceived by illusions, mind after mind without gap, movement and stillness as one. Eighth, he must press straight ahead with his thought, and must not use the mind to wait for awakening. Ninth, he must be long-enduring: until his will reaches the field of the ancients, he will never be content to stop. He must not be satisfied with a little. Tenth, within the work, thought after thought he must let go and desist. Let go of letting go; desist from desisting. Let go until there is nothing left to let go; desist until there is nowhere left to desist — and he will naturally see good news. If a student applies his mind thus, he will come somewhat into accord with his own original matter. One whose will is directed upward should encourage himself with this.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Liaoxin Hai

We who leave home do so solely for the great matter of birth and death. To travel with staff in hand, to visit teachers and seek out friends, is only to decide the one road that goes upward from beneath one’s own feet — and not to be satisfied until it is clear. Hence the good teacher presents people with this matter alone. In recent times the Dharma gate has fallen desolate, and this spirit is seldom heard in any quarter. Wherever the pilgrim goes, there is nothing but the breath of gruel and rice. The Elder was lodging at the Linghu hermitage when the Chan monk Liaoxin came to consult him. Entering the gate, I saw that he had the nose of a patch-robed monk and seemed not to be an ordinary eater of gruel. Now he was about to return to Funiu, and so he offered incense and asked for instruction. The Elder said to him: In the Chan groves within the seas today, the first thing to rely on is the ascetic practice of Niushan; no other quarter can match it. If a student of the Way can risk and cast aside body and life, his one life will certainly not be passed in vain. As for the work of daily use, taking up a single thought of huatou is the most dense and unbroken. The reason you cannot transcend and attain great freedom is that you have been dead-set on guarding the huatou, never letting it go thought after thought, and do not know that in Chan investigation the first requirement is to shed body and mind inwardly and leave the world behind outwardly — the one point of detachment from thought. Therefore your tied-up thought becomes a bond of thought instead, and you cannot transcend into great freedom. This time, when you enter the mountain, you are fortunate to rely on the rules and the support of the assembly; it is just right to take hold of the situation and put your strength to work. Simply, within each thought, watch the place before the thought arises — this lies in the one point of detachment from thought. After a long time the thought will suddenly snap; mind and objects will both be forgotten, and you will be like a lion slipped from its rope, roaming at ease. When you next see the Elder, your eyebrows and eyes in movement and stillness will certainly not be as they are today.
Instructions to the Upāsakas of Xiangtan

While the Buddha dwelt in the world and taught the Dharma, there were the four assemblies who constantly followed him. The two who left home were the bhikṣu and the bhikṣuṇī; the two who remained at home were the upāsaka and the upāsikā. These are rendered as “male lay-server” and “female lay-server,” because, being at home and able to keep the five precepts, they can serve the Three Jewels closely and are fit to receive the benefit of Dharma. So when the Buddha-Dharma came east, people received its teaching as the times allowed, and each generation had such people. Some indeed understood the mind and saw the nature and entered the Patriarchs’ chamber. In recent times the Dharma way has long been buried, and the transmission has no eye; people bow three times at random, receive a name by routine, and call themselves disciples. In truth their fishy smell has not been spat out and their old conduct is unchanged, which gives rise to mockery and slander, brings no benefit at all, and is a great cause of destroying the Dharma. Therefore the Elder never dared to grant this lightly in his life. Now, observing the disciples of Xiangtan, their faith is sincere and deep, not the drifting of the common stream, and so I have with difficulty consented to their request. But I think that you have never before heard the Dharma; though you are called good people, you do not know what makes one good. Now, according to the Treatise on Consciousness-Only, the mental factors number fifty-one, and the wholesome dharmas are only eleven; the rest are all unwholesome mental factors. The eleven are: faith, diligence, shame, remorse, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, pliancy, non-carelessness, equanimity of action, and non-harming. With all eleven complete, one is a purely good person; lacking even one, one is deficient in virtue. If you can simply receive and keep these wholesome dharmas according to the teaching, investigate each one clearly, and at all times observe and keep them in mind — where a dharma is not yet pure and familiar, apply more of the work of grinding and polishing, and strive to make it perfectly good and only then stop — then such application of mind makes one a truly good person. What is called the good mind is simply the pure true mind. All living beings each originally possess the Tathāgata’s pure true mind, but it is defiled by evil thoughts, and so they follow feeling and create karma without knowing it. If one can now observe the good mind, then all evil dharmas will not appear before him of themselves, and the mind will be pure of itself. If you have the will to observe deeply step by step, then just investigate the Sixth Patriarch’s public case in which he taught Huiming: “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — at that very moment, what is the Original Face of the Venerable Ming?” Investigate it at all times; this is called the road that goes upward. Beneath your heels, who is there without a foot of ground? Press forward with effort, and you will certainly not be cheated. If you are willing to turn your hearts to the Pure Land, then rely on this method and recite the Buddha’s name with one mind; then in this life you may cut off birth and death and forever end your sinking. But I fear only that a thieving mind deceives itself and cannot do the true practice. The Elder has forced himself to speak to you thus — for pity of a three-year-old child, he does not spare his two eyebrows. On no account take this as a worldly saying to be bandied about.
Instructions to Fang Juezhi (Yimao Year)

Fangzi Juezhi was deformed in body, yet the heavenly impulse within him wondrously unfolded. He came to consult the Elder at Nanyue, and the Elder saw that his mind-light shone brightly, that he was one who had long planted the seeds of prajñā, and often showed him what lies upward. Fangzi received it in his heart as if drinking ice. Now he was about to take leave and offered incense to ask for instruction. So the Elder said to him: Fangzi, do not think that Heaven has made your nature whole while crippling your form, and count that a defect. I know that Heaven does not burden you with form, but in truth thickens your virtue. In the world those whose forms are whole are many, yet those whose forms harm their lives are more still. Who can leave form behind and put aside intellect to make his nature whole? The sage called form a burden to life and said, “The great trouble is that I have a body.” Therefore he extinguished the body and returned to non-being, so that with the form dissolved suffering ceased. Our Buddha taught living beings to take the breaking of self as the highest principle. The essentials of entering Chan do not rely on the bodily frame, nor on breath — all is left behind, and the mind is still of itself. When the mind is still, no joy can compare with it. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “You should contemplate this body as a false union of the four great elements. What is hard returns to earth, what is moist returns to water, what is warm returns to fire, what moves returns to wind. When the four great elements separate, where will this false body be?” From now on, Fangzi, day and night you should simply contemplate in this way. Contemplate to the place where not a single thought arises: then outwardly you do not see a body, inwardly you do not see a mind; body and mind are still, utterly without a single dharma. At that time you will first know that Heaven took away your false body only to make your true one whole, and your supreme joy will arrive at its utmost without waiting to forget form. Only press on and contemplate thus; one day it will be transparently clear, and you will believe that the Elder’s words are not false.
Instructions to the Secretary Zhi Hai’an (Yimao Year)

While the Elder was at Wuyang teaching the Dharma, for a time the disciples of the Dharma-nature, both monks and laypeople, who took refuge were many, and the sight of them was fine to behold — it was a matter of time and conditions. Before long, however, there was much trouble, and it was hard to gather the Dharma assembly. The Elder entered Caoxi, and many of those who had been in the assembly also withdrew. Only Zhi Hai’an, Xiu Liuyi, and Ruo Xingjiong, these three, did not leave off attending him. And when he retired in old age to Nanyue, the two, An and Yi, followed without letting go. This shows the depth of their feeling for the milk of Dharma, and their sense of duty was of the highest. The Elder dwelt in seclusion east of the lake, and before he knew it three years had passed. His daily living was extremely plain, yet the two were content; I think the followers in Chen and Cai were no better than this. Lately An, because his teacher was old, returned home to pay his respects; he offered incense and asked for instruction, wishing to beg a single word to hold in practice for life. The Elder thought to himself that he was old, and that in the Dharma which transcends the world it is truly hard to come together; the scripture says, “Like a one-eyed turtle in the great ocean meeting the hole of a floating log” — how could that be easy? Alas, you are going; you should listen carefully. The Buddha said that all living beings have realized perfect enlightenment; know then that the Buddha-nature is complete in each person, lacking not a hair. Yet living beings wander in birth and death, and for long kalpas revolve without returning, simply because they turn their backs on enlightenment and join with dust, following the stream of birth and death and pursuing the net of demons without knowing it. Because they do not know or awaken themselves, they suffer sinking in vain — exactly like a beggar holding a pearl who does not know that the wish-fulfilling jewel is in his own bosom, and casts it away, gladly enduring his loneliness. For this reason the Tathāgata called them pitiable. The Elder has always observed that your nature is straightforward, that you forget contrivance and are near the Way; but your habits are deep and thick and you cannot hold yourself, and you are often bitterly dragged along by old habits. Once you enter the snare of demons, you fall wholly, and in your suffering you do not know it; and when you suddenly recollect, you hate that you cannot leap out of birth and death. Then you busily pack up and prepare to practice, but the conditions of the Way are not yet gathered, the familiar state appears before you, habit rises again, and before you know it you follow the waves. By the time you turn your head to look after it, much time has passed. Rising and falling like this, leaning on the Elder for twenty years, in the end the great matter of birth and death beneath your own feet has no landing place at all. Why is this? Because though you have the makings of one who enters the Way, the remaining portion of this passage is corrupted in the source. In substance it continues the Elder’s instruction to Hai’an on the essentials of settling the mind, on the work of one who dwells in the mountains, and on the practice of the assembly, urging him to cut off the old habits that have kept him turning in birth and death.
Instructions to Liu Cunchi (Yimao Year)

When I had retired in old age to Nanyue, at the close of winter in the jiayin year, Liu Jizi of Chaling came from afar to consult me. On a snowy night we sat around the stove, a cold lamp shining between us. I asked how he had been applying his mind. He replied: “Formerly I received the Master’s verse: ‘A lotus is born in fire; the world calls it rare. It is not that fire bears the lotus — it is only that the mind is apart from defilement.’ Looking at this saying, I have gained some use from the last line.” The Elder was deeply pleased and instructed him, saying: That you have gained power from the line “the mind is apart from defilement” — these words are not empty, and are not easy to reach either. The scripture says: “Ordinary being and sage, worthy and saint, are equal, with no high or low; it is only that the defilement of mind is extinguished, and the attainment is like turning the palm.” Seen from this, living beings and Buddhas are originally without two; what is called mind, Buddha, and living beings — these three are without difference. But when the mind is pure, one is Buddha; when the mind is defiled, one is a living being. The distance between living being and Buddha is not far: it lies only in whether the defilement of mind is extinguished or not. This mind is originally pure, but because of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, the five desires, afflictions, and all the illusions of karma, it is sullied and obscured — hence it is called a living being. If this defilement is purified, it is then called Buddha. How could this depend on another’s power? But there is no helping it: all living beings, from beginningless time, have deep and thick karmic obstruction and firm afflictions, and it is hard for them to become pure; they must rely on the work of polishing. Hence there are the various skillful means of Chan investigation, Buddha-recitation, and looking into the huatou — all of them medicines for curing the mind. It is like the light of a mirror, bright by nature, darkened by grime; one must rely on the medicine of polishing. Yet the medicine is also grime: it is used to remove that grime, and so when the mirror is bright the medicine is no longer there. Again, true gold in the ore has sand and stone, defilement and filth; there must be a method of smelting, and when the gold is pure there is no use for the smelting. The mind-defilement of living beings is hard to leave; one must apply diligent effort to adjust and cure it. When the defilement goes and the mind is bright, it is said that living beings are originally Buddha — not that one should, while wholly within affliction and turbid defilement, falsely call oneself Buddha. The path of Chan investigation and looking into the huatou is the most essential for clarifying the mind. But in recent times few take it in hand: partly because their faculties are dull, and they lack the ancients’ dead-set mind; partly because they have no true good teacher to decide and choose for them, and so most fall into false views. Therefore the practice of cultivating Buddha-recitation and Chan investigation together is an extremely safe Dharma gate. If you take one recitation of the Buddha’s name and keep it in your breast, thought after thought pursuing and examining where it arises and where it lands, determined to see exactly where it comes to rest, then after a long time the defilement will suddenly be purified and the brightness appear, and the ground of mind will open through. This is no different from looking into a public case or huatou; but it requires pressing hard to succeed. If you bob along on deluded thoughts and pass the days idly, treating it as a matter of no importance, then even at the end of your years you will gain no use from it. If you take idly indulging deluded thoughts as your use, then you deceive yourself — not only for one life, but from now on, even to the end of kalpas, there will be no time when you are not deceived. You have a karmic affinity with the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation; try to investigate it earnestly. In truth, amid the turbid defilement of affliction, one recitation of the Buddha’s name is like a pearl that clears the water; but to use it thus is not yet to reach the very source. The scripture says: “It is like settling turbid water: the sand and soil sink of themselves and clear water appears — this is called first subduing the afflictions of guest-dust. When the mud is gone and the water is pure, it is called forever cutting off fundamental ignorance.” Simply test yourself silently with these Buddha-words, and there will be no mistake. If you can reach the place of truly leaving defilement, then, as the scripture says, “the mark of clarity is pure and undefiled, and one is not obstructed by the afflictions of guest-dust.” In that case not only will Amitābha come to welcome you; all Buddhas of the ten directions will praise you with one voice. I am fortunate to have spent this whole year’s snowy night with you; this cool and plain family style is rare in the world. If you do not betray this good meeting, then simply, from now on, never let a thought depart from coolness and plainness — this is the one path out of defilement. Press on step by step, and there will surely come the time of true liberation, of arriving home.
Instructions to Zhong Hengying

Zhong Mingsheng of Chaling came from a family of scholars of the Odes and Rites. In the past, because of trouble and hardship, he traveled to Yue and consulted me at Caoxi. The Elder enlightened him with the teaching of the retribution of good and evil and of cause and effect, and set his mind at rest so that he could return; and in the end his trouble was resolved. The resolution of it was not something that could be reached by thought and imagination; the time and conditions happened to meet, and it came of itself without intent. Thereby his old possessions were unharmed, and he trod a ground of peace and quiet, free of affairs. Yet in the end he was wholly unaware why this was so, and still thought to use his strength of mind to seek the things that in his life had not yet satisfied his heart — as though reaching into a bag for something, or picking up a mustard seed. On the last day of the jiayin year he came with Liu Cunchi from afar to comfort me and to keep me company through the turning of the year. The Elder sighed and said: What you have set your will on is like crossing the sea and fording rivers to seek sweet spring water: the spring may not be found, and the thirst will only blaze the more, and you will have the toil of the journey besides. Did I not once teach you the principle of cause and effect and retribution? Have you forgotten it? Good and evil answer like shadow to form and echo to sound; when the voice is harmonious the echo follows, when the form is upright the shadow is straight. Hence the sage did not speak of cause and effect, but only said that for the good a hundred blessings descend, and for the not-good a hundred calamities. He took settling one’s destiny and steadying one’s will as the admonition. Hence it is said: “One who does not know destiny cannot be a gentleman.” The sage teaches people to settle their destiny; the Buddha teaches people to follow conditions — the way is one. To settle one’s destiny is to have not the least need to force anything; to follow conditions is to allow not a single thought of deluded imagining. Therefore the Buddha-Dharma teaches people to take cutting off deluded thought as the root. Deluded thought is the root of all evil karma — greed, hatred, delusion, and the rest. Even a bodhisattva’s practice up to Buddhahood, and the recompense of the most excellent adornments and vast fields of merit among gods and humans, all begin from cutting off deluded thought. For when deluded thought is cut off, evil karma dissolves; when evil karma dissolves, a hundred blessings gather. This is what is called seeking much blessing for oneself. Therefore he taught him with a verse: “All worldly things from deluded thought arise; where the deluded mind dissolves, karmic bonds grow light. You need not seek a further road to bodhi — only step back, just where you stand.” Stepping back is the highest work of resting the mind and cutting off delusion. For the human mind is originally bright and vast, the source of ten thousand blessings; but it is screened by deluded marks and evil karma, and so calamity daily grows and blessing daily decreases. If now delusion dissolves and karma is cut, then the one nature is perfect and bright, and its enjoyment is boundless; to attain that place of enjoyment is true blessing. Know then that blessing is made by oneself, and truly cannot be brought about by cleverness, craft, or scheming. Moreover, by cutting off the deluded mind, the Buddha moved gods and humans to blessing. Zhong Mingsheng has the foundation for merit, fame, wealth, and honor; if he can directly rest his mind and, from the beginning, carefully examine one by one all the karma he has made in his life, then wherever there is a thought that wrongs the heart, injures principle, or is not in accord with the great Way — all of it is a root of suffering; let him spit it all out and establish a new foundation. Make a fresh effort, and take resting the mind, cutting off delusion, and awaiting the time as your single standard. Give your mind to the enterprise you already possess, and do not seek further the things of a single deluded thought. Thus you will remedy the faults of your former course; one day calamity will dissolve and blessing arrive, and merit, fame, wealth, and honor will press in upon you with no place to retreat. What need then for all kinds of deluded thought and clinging to seek elsewhere? If Zhong Mingsheng can truly believe without doubt and hold to this in practice, then even the fruit of Buddhahood may be expected — how much more the conditions of the world? Strive, strive!
Instructions to Yuan Datu

Scholars and gentry in the world who have their will set upward and give their minds to studying the Buddha often think deeply and raise themselves high, casting off worldly affairs from afar and imitating the withered-tree ascetic as wondrous practice. They do not realize that the Buddha already sharply rebuked such people, calling them scorched sprouts and rotten seeds, meaning that they cannot enter the world to benefit living beings. This is exactly what the earlier Confucians pointed to as nihility and extinction, and our Buddha would not have tolerated it long ago. What Buddhism values lies in benefiting self and benefiting others; only then is one called a bodhisattva. The Sanskrit word bodhisattva is rendered as “being of the great mind,” because such a one can enter the realm of living beings and can cut off affliction, and so earns this name. Apart from the world a bodhisattva has no practice to cultivate; apart from living beings he has no instrument for cutting off affliction. Therefore the bodhisattva relies on living beings to cut off the afflictions of his own nature. It is like the stone of another mountain, which can polish one’s jade. Affliction means greed, hatred, self-love, views, pride, and all kinds of bad habits, which obstruct the light of one’s own nature. Without all the adverse conditions and situations of living beings in the world, one cannot grind and cut them away. This is what the Odes mean by “cut and file, carve and polish.” Moreover, the Buddha’s five precepts are the five constants of the Confucians: not killing is benevolence; not stealing is righteousness; not committing sexual misconduct is propriety; not drinking wine is wisdom; not speaking falsely is faithfulness. Only because they come from the Buddha’s own mouth, the words differ while the meaning is the same. People today often make a vow to receive the Buddha’s precepts, yet of themselves neglect the five constants — they know two fives but not ten. They also exalt Chan concentration as the highest vehicle because it can clarify the mind and reveal the nature, not knowing that the Confucians have this too. When Yan Yuan asked about benevolence, the Master said, “To overcome oneself and return to propriety is benevolence.” The self is the grasping of self — is this not first breaking self-grasp as the essential of Chan cultivation? “One day overcoming oneself, and the whole world returns to benevolence” — is this not the wonder of sudden awakening? For the whole world consists of things set against oneself as opposing obstacles; if self-grasp is once broken, then all things are oneself — is not “returning to benevolence” the effect of sudden awakening? And when he asked directly for its particulars, the Master said, “Do not look, listen, speak, or move contrary to propriety” — because what one looks at, listens to, speaks, and moves among are all things and not propriety, and so they are one’s obstruction. To say “do not” means not to be turned about by sound and form; in all places not to fall into impropriety — is this not entering Chan with precepts first? But the Buddha mostly spoke in terms of leaving the world, yet what he practiced was never apart from the world; even what a bodhisattva dwelling in the world practices is no other than this. Buddha means awakened: to be able to awaken this mind is to be named Buddha; it is not that apart from this pure mind one seeks another Buddha. It is just that living beings’ bad habits and obstructions are heavy and their minds are hard to purify; therefore the skillful means of Buddha-recitation is established, and the Dharma gate of seeking birth in the Pure Land. And it is said, “When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.” Know then that Buddha-recitation is indeed a wondrous practice for purifying the mind. But Buddha-recitation is fundamentally for purifying the mind; if one recites the Buddha’s name and yet one’s mind is not pure, what is the use of reciting? If one keeps the precepts while turning one’s back on the five constants, what is the use of the precepts? Master Yuan has his will set on the Way and has formed a fellowship to cultivate the pure karma together — this surely issues from good roots long planted. He came to see the Elder and firmly asked to receive the precepts. The Elder instructed him, saying: The precepts are originally complete in one’s own nature. If you truly believe the Elder’s words and purify your own mind, then the precepts are already received, Chan is already cultivated, the Pure Land is already entered, and the bodhisattva’s wondrous practice, the worldly and world-transcending dharmas, and the two benefits are all complete — none of it goes beyond this. Strive at it, sir.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Shuanglun Zhao

The Chan monk Shuanglun Zhao came to consult me, saying that he intended to withdraw into the mountains and investigate the matter that goes upward alone, and asking the Elder for the method of dwelling in the mountains. So the Elder instructed him, saying: For the ancients, dwelling in the mountains was a place of great renunciation of body and life — by no means a small matter. It requires above all that one be good at using the mind. As for the method of using the mind: first, take up the single thought that goes upward and plant your stance firmly at the place where Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot allow you. Next, you must spit out all the knowledge and views and the wondrous words and wondrous sayings in your breast, as so much mixed poison. Next, you must recognize that the original substance is utterly without a single dharma, and must not let the shadows of deluded thought and habit produce all kinds of states that confuse and disorder right mindfulness. Next, you must look into your root huatou — such as the Sixth Patriarch’s public case, “not thinking of good, not thinking of evil; what is your Original Face?” — and hold it up with all your strength. Whenever any bad habit appears before you, at once see through it with the phrase “from the first not a single thing exists.” On no account follow it on in unbroken succession; clench your teeth, for here you must hold your ground, and only then will you not be shaken or robbed by it. Using the mind thus is the place of effort when you are alert. If you use the mind with too much effort, then laziness arises and drowsiness sets in. At such a time you must simply brighten up quickly and not fall into the pit of torpor. You must quickly recite a mantra: relying on the power of the mantra, you can match this demon. For in the storehouse consciousness there are bad habits from many kalpas, and now they are squeezed out by the huatou and transform into inexhaustible states. All demonic states arise from deluded thought; all torpor arises from scatteredness. Just when you are using the mind rightly, a single scattered thought at once falls into torpor — this you must know well. Yongjia’s fourfold criterion of stillness and alertness is the most essential. The ancients, in using the mind, simply leaned steadily on one phrase of root huatou, as if it were an iron wall and a silver mountain. If you reach the place where not a single thought arises, that too is a sign of power, but do not take it as the ultimate. Only when the work goes on effortlessly and no longer depends on thought, and with one thought it opens clear and body and mind seem to fall away empty — only that is the place where the work takes hold; and even that is not yet the ultimate. But if you can reach this, you will naturally be light and at ease and will give rise to joy. Yet this is only the original matter, not something extraordinary. If you give rise to the thought that it is extraordinary, you fall into the demon of joy, and you will start producing groundless wild knowing and wild understanding. This pass is the most dangerous; these are things the Elder has tested. The ancients said: “Before the withered tree and the cliff, wrong roads are many; travelers who reach here all stumble away their time.” This is no small matter. Even if you have the strength to fight through all kinds of states, that is just the time to practice and the time to protect; it is not yet arriving home. If you take this as enough, you will start giving rise to thoughts of all the worldly conditions of the five desires. This pass is hard to cross; of those who cross it, not one or two in a hundred. That is why one does not reach the ancients’ field — it is precisely the fault of being satisfied with a little. Even if a student works bitterly for a lifetime and reaches this ground, if he is dragged off by such bad habits he still falls into the pit of birth and death, and all his previous work is lost. Is this not lamentable? Sayings such as this are not few in the records of the ancients. The Elder has picked out a few, because in the Dharma-ending age it is hard to find a true student of the Way — it is also that, having once been a prodigal myself, I pity the traveler. On the whole, the ancients’ dwelling in the mountains was not to nurse laziness and seek comfort; it was solely for the great matter of their own birth and death. Therefore they went into ten thousand layers of cold cliffs and made their living without any device. If one dawdles away the days here and wastes the light of time for nothing, is that not still more pitiable? Nevertheless, the differences in using the mind you now know. As for the shifting conditions before you in the mountains — the water flowing, the wind moving, gibbons crying, birds calling, clouds rising, mist gathering, crowding before you, even more clamorous — Yongjia’s saying about seeing the Way and forgetting the mountain must be seen through. When the Elder first dwelt at Longmen in Wutai, beneath ten-thousand-fathom cold cliffs, in piles of ice and snow, I was like a dead man buried; the cold pierced to the bone and penetrated all five organs, and only a faint breath remained, and I watched it come and go through the ice. At this point, turning the light back, I sought the place where a single thought of my own mind arose and could not find it. This state is exactly a condition that aids the Way. Again, when the great wind blew, ten thousand apertures roared with rage, day and night without rest; and when the snow melted and the torrents ran, the sound was like rolling thunder, and again like a thousand troops and ten thousand horses galloping. Such confused states were hardest to bear at first. Then I thought of the ancients’ saying: “If one listens to the sound of water for thirty years without turning the faculty of mind, one may be permitted to enter the Way.” So the Elder made a furious resolve and sat and stood on a single-plank bridge, listening to the sound of the water all day. At first it was clattering and hard to dissolve; after a long time it was indeed suddenly stilled. From then on all states were stilled. What is called “the ten thousand states are originally at leisure; it is only people who make their own clamor” — this again is the first piece of work for a person of the Way dwelling in the mountains. Let the Chan monk remember it and not neglect it.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Zhuanyu Heng (Bingchen Year)

The road that goes upward is the original matter of one who has left home. When the ancients set out to surpass the ordinary, it was only to investigate this matter clearly. In recent times people generally do not know what leaving home is for; how can one expect them to be like the ancients? The Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng first relied on Master Kongyin of Wutai and studied the scriptures and treatises. After a long time he swept them all aside and took up the single thought, earnestly investigating his original matter. He traveled ten thousand li to the south, passed through Caoxi, and paid his respects to the Elder, asking for instruction. The Elder told him: If in this matter you do not put down body and mind and investigate with bitter effort to the place where the water runs out and the mountains end, there will in the end be no landing place. And even if you reach the place where the water runs out and the mountains end, the ancients called this “still, sunken, dead water,” and also “the wondrous nest.” If you do not turn your head and turn your brain around, then what is before you will be like an iron wall and a silver mountain — that is only the time of power, not the place of use. The ancients’ use of mind was not to die all the way to the bottom; one must be able to come alive within death. The essential is to turn the mechanism and shift the position. Therefore it is said: “The one who sits at the top of a hundred-foot pole has indeed entered, but is not yet real. Let him step forward from the top of the hundred-foot pole, and the whole universe appears in his body.” When a student reaches this, he must simply turn around and walk another road, and only then will it not become an obstruction to him. The Chan monk assented, bowed, and departed. He went to cut thatch at Nanyue. Before long the Elder too came dragging his staff, and asked after the monk, who had been harried by the demon of sickness and had already gone to Baoqing for medical treatment. Hearing this the Elder sighed and said: The Chan gate is in decline, and a student who truly works for birth and death is the hardest thing to find. Now this man has this illness — is it that the dragons and gods are weary of the Dharma gate? On the first day of the third month of spring in the bingchen year, at midnight amid wind and rain, the monk suddenly came, braving the rain and plunging through the mud. The Elder was overjoyed to see him and said: This is not something a sick man could do. Seeing the fresh, clear spirit in his brows and face, he knew that his illness was eight or nine parts cured. Then the monk again offered incense and asked for instruction. The Elder specially taught him, saying: Your demon of sickness is your great good teacher, a condition that aids the Way. Do you know this? Consider: the sickness of living beings lies in having a self. Because they grasp a self, all afflictions and all sicknesses arise from it. When sickness arises, suffering must follow. From ancient times to now there is no one who is not sick in this way; only the person who knows that sickness is sickness is not sickened by it. Moreover, this body is a false union of the four great elements; what is gathered must scatter. Even if you were not ill now, would you not in fact be ill? If you understand that the sick one is not sick, then sickness cannot sicken him. You know today’s illness, but you do not know that through many lives and kalpas, illness after illness has come down to today. If you do not settle today’s illness, then from now on you will not know where illness ends. You know the sickness of birth and death, but you do not know that you must escape the sickness of birth and death — and that is a much greater sickness than birth and death itself. Why? The ancients said that if Chan investigation does not get out of the realm of the aggregates but falls into the pit of consciousness and feeling, then even a wondrous awakening becomes the view of self. If one grasps the four great elements as self, the sickness can still be treated. But if one leaves the four great elements and still grasps a self, this sickness leaves even the king of physicians helpless; it is the hardest of all to cure. All Buddhas and Patriarchs came into the world expressly to cure this one disease of the vital organs. They spent how much effort, yet how many are there who are willing to take the medicine and be cured? The monk’s bodily illness is cured — on no account let him be invaded by the illness of Chan. Yunmen said the dharma-body has two kinds of illness. He said that one may pass through the dharma-body, but if the grasping of dharmas is not forgotten and one’s own views still remain, that too is illness — a strong statement about the illness of clinging and grasping. Let the Chan monk spit out all the wondrous words and wondrous sayings he formerly held, along with the merit he has accumulated in clinging to Chan investigation, until not a single bad perception or bad habit remains. Then it will surely not grow into a root of illness. It will even leave the Buddhas and Patriarchs with no place to stand. Have you not heard of the youth Sudhana, who traveled south through a hundred cities and consulted fifty-three great good teachers, each bestowing a different Dharma gate, and in the end came only to being equal to the dharma-realm, equal to space? Was there ever a real dharma to which he was tied? And have you not heard of Vairocana, whose dharma-body is no body, but who takes the wondrous practice of Samantabhadra as his body? Samantabhadra has no practice; he takes the practice of living beings as his practice. Therefore it is said: “What bodhi takes as its condition is living beings in suffering; if there were no living beings, there would be no bodhi.” This is the true model of how the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the lineage came into the world. Therefore the Elder said to the monk: Your body of four great elements is sick, and only the demon of sickness can cure it; the illness of Chan pierces the heart, and only living beings can cure it. From today on, simply make your body equal to the great earth, and the demon of sickness will hide its traces; make your mind equal to living beings, and the view of self will not stand. When the view of self does not stand, the illness of Chan dissolves of itself. For when the mind does not take itself as mind, it is fundamentally unborn; being unborn, not a single dharma is established. If not a single dharma is established, what dharma is there to become an obstruction of views? The ancients said: “It is easy to renounce feeling; it is hard to renounce dharmas.” When the monk renounces body he renounces feeling; when he renounces views he renounces dharmas. With feeling and dharmas both forgotten, will he not be a person of great unobstructed liberation? Alas, I am old, and to meet again will be hard. Strive, monk.
Instructions to Li Fujing

Li Yingzhen of Lingling asked for instruction on the purport of mind and nature. So the Elder taught him, saying: What are mind and nature? They are the great root of all sages and ordinary beings, of all living things. Because the substance is the same while the function differs, there is the difference between delusion and awakening, and hence the distinction between the real and the deluded. It is said that the three realms are mind only and the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only. Because one mind is deluded, it becomes consciousness; and consciousness is purely the functioning of delusion, pursuing objects and clinging to conditions, no longer knowing the true mind that is originally possessed. But if one knows that the true is originally possessed and understands that the deluded is fundamentally nonexistent, then one can return from delusion to the real, and from the realm of living beings one may at once enter the realm of the Buddha. When Bodhidharma came from the west, he transmitted only the mind-seal, the Dharma gate of sudden awakening — precisely awakening suddenly to this mind. This is the purport of the Chan school concerning mind, nature, the real, and the deluded. As for what our Confucians revere, the mind and nature transmitted by Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius: they say, “Only the refined, only the one,” taking refinement and oneness as the ultimate principle, and they distinguish the human mind from the mind of the Way — this too is a distinction between the real and the deluded. Only the teaching of the world does not go beyond this. What they call the mind of the Way is the nature that is not deluded and not false; what they call the human mind is the nature deluded into feeling. People in the world know only how to use feeling, not how to use nature; they know only the waves, not that the waves are originally water. Therefore Confucius said: “Natures are near; habits carry them far apart.” When nature is near, the water originally has no waves; when habit carries one far, one pursues the waves and forgets the water. One does not even know the water — how much less does one understand that the nature of wetness is without two? Take one body of water: mix it with salt, sour, bitter, and pungent, and its bland nature is lost, yet its wet nature is fundamentally without two. Know then that the many flavors are transformations of the deluded, while the wet nature cannot be transformed. What cannot be transformed is real; what can be transformed is deluded. If one understands that the wet nature is without two, then the many flavors cannot be had. This is what is meant by “Yao and Shun are the same as other people”: what is the same is the nature, what is not the same is the delusion. It is also said, “Everyone can be a Yao or a Shun.” What can be is the nature; what cannot be is habit. As for people’s habits, if one abandons the low and defiled and inclines to the high and bright, then daily one moves away from one’s habits and nearer to the nature — and it is by this habit too that one can become a Yao or a Shun. Habit nearing the nature is what the Chan school means by gradual cultivation. Because the learning of the worldly Confucians has not left the ordinary and near and is still far from the sage, without gradual advance one cannot reach the utmost. Therefore the sage established his teaching with only “habit,” “arriving,” and “overcoming”; his work of entering the Way lies in gradual restoration, and he did not speak of sudden awakening. But the Chan gate sets aside the love of wife and children and removes the desire for wealth and honor; with all burdens already released, one is close to the Way. Therefore the work of restoring the nature is easy to accomplish, and so it is called sudden awakening. Because the ground on which one stands differs, the cultivation is easy or hard. In truth, as for mind and nature in a person, there is fundamentally no difference of sudden or gradual; one speaks only of the thickness or thinness of habitual defilement. This is the essential of entering the Way. If one investigates the subtlety of mind and nature and traces it to its source: what Chan takes as its root is the unborn and undying; what the Confucians take as their root is birth and death. Hence it is said, “Generation and regeneration is called the Changes.” This is the distinction between the roots of Confucianism and Buddhism. The doctrine of mind and nature lies here. As for the one point that goes upward in the Chan gate, it transcends speech and language, and does not take mind and nature as a real dharma either.
Instructions to the Censor Jia Huanran, Who Asked for Guidance

The Buddhas came into the world, yet there is no dharma they could speak; the Patriarch came from the west, yet he had no real dharma to give people. It was only to smash, as was fitting, the various inverted and clinging feelings of living beings, to make them let go of clinging and suddenly awaken to what they originally possess. Because living beings’ minds of deluded clinging are firm and hard to break, and are further deepened by beginningless ignorance, affliction, and karmic obstruction, sudden awakening is hard to attain; hence our Buddha spent forty-nine years and measureless skillful means establishing the dharma of cutting off delusion and realizing the truth. From ordinary being to sage, he set up fifty-five stages of gradation. It is not that the World-Honored One liked to make such arrangements and spend his grandmotherly heart. Because the sicknesses of living beings’ minds are measureless, the prescriptions to match them are measureless too. When one arrives at ultimate reality, until knowing and seeing are utterly extinguished and not a single dharma is established, only then is it the ground of arriving home. If even a hair of knowing and seeing is not forgotten, one is still outside the gate, lodging in a thatched hut. Cast it away and cast it away until there is nothing left to cast away — and even then, this is still a matter on the side of the dharma-body, not the matter of the dharma-body going upward. It is only the utmost limit of the teaching schools, not the utmost limit of the Chan gate. Seen thus, is practice a careless thing, to be taken as attainment on the strength of a half-understanding? Moreover, in the Chan gate before the Sixth Patriarch the work of investigation was not spoken of; only sudden awakening here and now was valued. From Nanyue and Qingyuan onward, people’s faculties were not uniform, and most relied on investigation and nurturing. When the five houses were established, their gateways and arrangements differed, but the essential purport within them was originally without difference. As for responding to capacities and receiving people, they were like the Qin mirror on its stand, reflecting through to the liver and gall. As for loosening people’s adhesions and removing their bonds, pointing directly to the dharma-body and the road that goes upward, and wiping out the knowing and seeing of Buddha-Dharma — until the source was exhausted and the bottom reached, they absolutely would not let it pass lightly. In the time when the Chan way was greatly flourishing there were many clear-eyed teachers in the world, and students of the Way consulted and verified everywhere, so that those who awakened did not fall into false views. By the Song and Yuan, though teachers were many, students’ false views were not few: if they did not fall into birth and death, they fell into the view of emptiness, having substance but no function, like the two vehicles’ one-sided emptiness. Some even denied cause and effect and fell into the outsiders’ libertine nihilism. Or their awakening of mind was not thorough, and seeing a mere glimmer they were satisfied with a little, calling themselves bodhisattvas, talking of emptiness with every mouth while their minds clung to existence, and so creating the karma of birth and death without knowing it. In all such cases they had no clear-eyed teacher to examine and press them; hence the Chan gate withered. The ancients said, “It is not that there is no Chan; it is only that there are no teachers” — this is what they meant. On the whole, in the Dharma-ending age those who investigate Chan and are satisfied with a little are many. Even if there is a true student willing to work with a dead-set hand, unchanging in his will for ten or five years, and he comes to understand that his own mind is utterly empty, because he has no clear teacher to verify him he falls into the view of emptiness. Or his consciousness-spirit is not yet broken and he falls into the doorway of lights and shadows. Or his habits are not yet pure, and pressed by the work they manifest all kinds of states, which he takes for the wondrous functioning of spiritual powers. Or he sees Buddhas and bodhisattvas appear and teach the Dharma, or gains knowledge of others’ minds and of past lives and can see future events, or gives rise to all kinds of strange views. All these are transformations of habit; if one takes them as extraordinary, one falls into the demonic path. It is a pity that a whole stretch of work should do no small harm. All this comes from not meeting a clear teacher and not knowing the skillful means of cultivating the mind in the Buddha’s teaching, and so one falls into error. There are also those who truly investigate and truly awaken, clearly seeing that their own mind is utterly without a single dharma, but who cannot open the true eye at the crown of the head, and so sit in the place of bare nakedness, red and scattered, pure and clean and utterly without a point. This is called clinging to the top of the pole, still sunken dead water. Hence it is said: “The one who sits at the top of a hundred-foot pole has indeed entered, but is not yet real. Let him step forward from the top of the hundred-foot pole, and the whole universe appears in his body.” It is also said: “Where there is a Buddha, do not linger; where there is no Buddha, pass on quickly.” This is precisely to teach people that they must not sit inside the armor of no-affairs and then say there is no Buddha to attain and no living being to save — for this falls precisely into the view of annihilation and cannot leave this view of emptiness. Even if one reaches this, it is still a matter on the side of the dharma-body, not the matter of the dharma-body going upward. Have you not heard Yunmen say: “When you reach the side of the dharma-body, there seems dimly to be something there; this too is light not fully penetrating. Even if you penetrate it, to let it go is still not permitted”? These words are truly a mirror for cultivating the mind and seeing into the heart. Hence the ancients said: “The word ‘awakened’ must be spat out.” Know that the Buddhas and Patriarchs taught the Dharma with one flavor only: to dispel living beings’ clinging feelings. What is called simply exhausting ordinary feeling, with no other sagely understanding. If one makes a sagely understanding of it, one at once receives the host of demons. The fifty kinds of skandha-māras in the Śūraṅgama Sutra are not idle words. If practitioners today have no clear teacher to point the way and do not rely on the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ teachings for verification, what shall they use as their evidence? Originally, because living beings clung to existence, the Buddha broke their view of existence. Because the two vehicles and the outsiders clung to emptiness, the Buddha broke their view of emptiness. Because bodhisattvas clung to the two extremes of emptiness and existence, the Buddha taught neither emptiness nor existence to break the view of the two extremes. And when they entered the Buddha-Dharma, he further dispelled their Buddha-view and Dharma-view. Hence he dispelled until there was nothing to dispel. This is precisely “not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata.” Have you not heard of Sudhana, who consulted fifty-three great good teachers, entering the fifty-three Dharma gates and the Buddha’s realm, and who did not speak of the matter of becoming a Buddha, but only said “equal to space, equal to the dharma-realm, equal to Vairocana”? And when he met the bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the latter then taught him the ten kinds of conduct and vows. This is the great model of practicing the Way and learning Buddhahood: one does not treat post-awakening as a matter of no further affairs. If people today, though they can awaken thoroughly to the dharma-realm, do not learn Sudhana’s cultivation of Samantabhadra’s great conduct, in the end they cannot avoid falling into the outsiders’ view of emptiness. Should one not fear this? The tangled vines above are spoken especially for those who practice without much learning and wisdom, who apply their minds wrongly and cannot enter the Buddha’s knowing and seeing; hence I could not avoid wagging my tongue. If you regard them as idle words, you will not only betray this old monk but greatly deceive yourselves.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Yujue

The two Chan monks Huiyu and Huijue of Qiyang consulted the Elder at Ziyun Mountain in Huangmei. They said that in their minds birth and ceasing went on without a moment’s pause, like wild horses, and they especially sought instruction: how should they subdue their minds? The Elder taught them, saying: A student practices for the great matter of birth and death. Because thought after thought in the mind does not stop, birth and death are unbroken. If you truly want to end birth and death, you must let go of all ten thousand conditions utterly, until they are clean and gone. But there are seeds of beginningless habit that cannot be cleaned away; you must investigate a huatou. There are such things on paper, but you do not know the method for the difficulty or ease of taking it in hand; you must consult a good teacher, who will teach you the skillful means, because he has walked that road and knows the easy place to enter. For example, the Sixth Patriarch, hearing “let the mind arise without dwelling on anything,” awakened on the spot. People in the world do not understand this and take it as some wondrous principle. It was originally nothing wondrous: because he formerly had dwelling, and now heard of non-dwelling, he let go at that moment and so awakened. What is wondrous about it? Take Master Yongming: formerly he applied his mind to Buddha-recitation and could not enter; later, before Weituo, he drew lots and obtained Buddha-recitation. People in the world take Chan as a principle to be discussed, not knowing that Chan is one’s own mind. The scripture says, “unborn and undying” — this is it. If you want to understand the great matter of birth and death, know that the precepts are honored and you must never dare to transgress them. First you must have the strength of faith, a willing mind, and a firm resolve, and put down all wondrous words and wondrous principles, worldly affairs, and human feelings. This one point of Chan investigation is originally without anything wondrous or extraordinary. This matter is extremely simple — will you believe it? If you truly will, then simply put down all your former deluded thoughts at once and do not allow them to creep up. Slowly take up one recitation of Amitābha Buddha and lean on it steadily. You must watch where this thought arises, like letting down a fishing line into a deep pool. If deluded thoughts arise again, it is because beginningless habit is too heavy; you must let go again. On no account use the mind to cut off deluded thoughts; simply straighten your backbone, do not think east or west, and look fixedly right at the place where the deluded thought arises. Let go and let go again; slowly raise the Buddha’s name once more, and firmly watch where this one recitation of the Buddha ultimately arises from. After five or seven recitations the deluded thoughts will not arise. Then bring down the doubt: examine just who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. People in the world take this as a mere phrase; they do not know that only here, in bringing down this doubt, lies the place of power. If deluded thoughts arise again, then shout “Tut!” and just ask who it is — and the deluded thought will at once vanish without trace. The Buddha said, “Except when sleeping, always gather the mind.” When sleeping you cannot gather the mind; as soon as you wake, take up the huatou. Not only when sitting, but walking, standing, drinking tea and eating, in movement and stillness, do the same. In a dense crowd, do not see that there are people; amid all movements, do not see that there is movement. Thus you will gradually have a place of entry, and the seventh consciousness will not function here. Lean steadily on it day and night thus, not counting the effort, and one day the eighth consciousness will suddenly burst open and expose your Original Face — that is the time of ending birth and death, and only then will you not betray the resolve with which you left home. But when investigating Chan, do not seek awakening. Let the Buddha come, let the Patriarch come, let demons come — simply do not move. Take up the single thought and walk on; let there be no further doubt in between. Thus dense and unbroken, mind after mind without gap, put forth effort in daily use, and there will surely be a landing place.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Mingyi

A student does not know the road that goes upward, but seeks only to increase his knowledge and views. He does not realize that to establish knowing upon knowing is the root of ignorance. This is not knowing what one originally possesses, and rushing out to seek it elsewhere, wishing further to increase one’s clarity. But if one clarifies that clarity, then clarity too is not established — what increase is there? Hence it is said, “In pursuit of learning one daily increases.” Whoever speaks of learning looks for a nest of comfort in someone else’s house. Even if he finds it, it is in the end not his own. Since it is not his own, the joy is not true joy; and if the joy is not true, how can he be at peace in it? To seek peace outside oneself is the common disease of students since ancient times, not only today. The Chan monk Mingyi asked for instruction. Would he say there is no benefit, and wish to clarify it? Or that there is benefit, and wish to clarify it? If you say there is no benefit, then with no benefit there is no need. If you say there is benefit, then since there is already benefit, why need clarify it? Try to see from what clarity is clarified and from what benefit benefits. If you seek to clarify your clarity, you lose the original clarity; if you seek still more benefit, it turns into no benefit. Whoever seeks benefit is like a man already full who still craves the flavor, and so harms his digestion and brings on illness. If he can vomit up what he has eaten, he may recover without medicine. If he guards his illness and avoids the doctor, it will end in a lump and a stoppage. Whoever is sick in this way, even Bian Que and Li Zhu could not cure. Why? To crave food and not vomit it is the first illness; to nurse the illness and hide the disease is the second; when the illness is full-blown, to avoid the doctor is the third; to go further and hate the medicine is the fourth; to seek a quick effect, distrusting the prescription that cures the root, and so to doubt the doctor and abandon the medicine is the fifth; and to take poison by mistake from a quack doctor, so that life is harmed — this is the incurable category. A student who abandons his original clarity and rushes out to seek, increasing his knowledge and views, is mostly like this. How sad! When I was young, each time I read the parable of the physician I never failed to repeat the sage’s teaching three times. I observe that students in recent times, as soon as they become novices, can recite this — yet in old age they do not know the source, and so there is no limit to those who waste their lives for nothing. This is the fault of not understanding. There are also those who seek clarity but mistakenly force the unclear to be clear for them — truly the fault of not reaching the root. The Buddha said: “Rest the mind and reach the root; therefore one is called a śramaṇa.” If a student can rest the mind and reach the root, clarity need not be sought outside and benefit need not be much increased; the self-nature is complete — where has it ever been deficient? If the Chan monk Mingyi can truly know this and at once spit out all the many places he formerly sought, then, like a man whose food-injury has left no residue in his belly, his original vitality will restore itself. When a student scrapes away knowing and seeing, he may be called a person of the Way with no affairs. Try carefully to examine the bellyful of sour stuff you had before, and see what flavor it has. Investigate! Investigate!
Instructions to the Chan Monk Huileng

The Chan monk was born and grew up in the town of Xiu. When young he traded on the rivers and lakes, and because he wearied of the dust and vulgarity he went to Mount Kuang and took the tonsure under Master Xufang. The Elder came from Nanyue to spend the summer at Jinzhu. The monk offered incense and asked for instruction. So the Elder taught him, saying: You have been able to renounce the world’s affection and love; your body has left home, but your mind does not yet understand what leaving home means. Formerly our Buddha, the World-Honored One, gave up the golden wheel, abandoned the royal palace, entered the Snow Mountains, and practiced austerities for six years; seeing the morning star he awakened to the Way, accomplished perfect enlightenment, and became the teacher of the three realms, revered by the six paths, honored and supported by gods and humans, saving all living beings and bringing them out of birth and death together. This is the very first model of leaving home. Seen thus, is leaving home a matter of stealing ease and nursing laziness, prizing ready-made comfort? There must be an original matter in it. The Patriarchs of the lineage left home for the great matter of birth and death; as for traveling with staff in hand and consulting good teachers, it was especially to bring the mind-ground to clarity and to pull out by the root the plant of birth and death accumulated through measureless kalpas, so as to transcend the three realms and forever leave the bitter destinies — this is benefiting oneself. Afterward, when the dragons and gods pushed one forth and one established the Three Jewels, that is benefiting others. With the two benefits complete, this is the original matter of leaving home. Today, monk, you have left home — have you known of this matter? Have you known the great matter of birth and death? What is birth and death? It is this present body and mind of the five aggregates, gathered from beginningless kalpas with every kind of seed of habit — greed, hatred, delusion, pride, aversion, and craving. The mind that day by day gives rise to delusion and creates karma is originally the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature, a seed of light; now it is covered by ignorance and affliction, and one does not know it in daily use. Thus to be deluded about this Buddha-nature is birth and death; to awaken to this Buddha-nature and at once cut off affliction and escape birth and death is to be a true child of the home-leaver. Seen thus, leaving home is a great man’s matter of ending birth and death, not the enjoyment of comfort or the prizing of ease. To refuse to practice, to not seek to clarify the mind and see the nature, is to consume the offerings of the faithful in vain and to invite in return the suffering of repayment in a future life. What leaving home is there in that? Monk, from what birth, by what conditions, by what fortune have you met a clear teacher to save and liberate you, and dwell at ease in a famous mountain’s monastery with Dharma companions in harmony? And again, how fortunate to meet a good teacher to guide and instruct you! If you do not give rise to deep rejoicing and great shame, and resolve with firm will to practice and seek to escape birth and death, then you abandon yourself — like going to a mountain of treasures and returning empty-handed. Is that not pitiable? Monk, if you are willing to rouse your will and practice, you must first cut off at once all your former afflictions, aversion, craving, and habits; single-mindedly seek only the one point of ending birth and death; and take the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” and keep it in your breast as your own root of life, mind after mind unbroken. Recite until the flower opens and you see the Buddha: that is the true time of ending birth and death and truly leaving home. If you do not take the Elder’s words and rouse true faith, you will be avoiding drowning by jumping into fire; this life will be missed, and when will there be a time of getting out? Think for yourself and encourage yourself. Do not neglect it.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Banji Wen

The Chan monk studied the examinations’ learning in his youth, but had the will to leave the world. At forty he abandoned wife and children and paid homage to Master Guoqing Zhan, a disciple of Elder Zibo, and was ordained at Guizong. Guizong was the Chan cave where the venerable elders of old established the banner of Dharma, and the Buddha’s relics are there. Know then that the conditions of the monk’s leaving home were excellent and the place he dwells in is excellent; it is only that he has not roused an excellent mind. Guizong had long been in ruins. When Master Zibo passed that way he was grief-stricken and sorrowful; seeing a withered pine half broken by axe and bill, the Master in compassion chanted a spell and banked earth about it, hoping it would flourish again, and using it to divine whether the monastery would be rebuilt. Within a few years its bark and wood were whole again. Thereupon Master Zhan resolutely raised it anew. When people far and near heard of it, there was none who did not look up in wonder and follow. The layman Xing Laici vowed his heart to lead the way. A few more years passed, and the present Emperor was moved to bestow the imperial canon to glorify the famous mountain; and so the halls and pavilions were completed. Then the Elder Jianyin raised funds to make a great Vairocana image to settle and secure it. From this the Three Jewels had two of their number; only the Jewel of the Saṅgha was not yet gathered, and so it was not enough to spread the way of Dharma. In the eighth year since the monk left home, the Elder came from Nanyue on a visit and paid homage to the relics on the summit of the Golden Wheel Peak. He saw the excellence of its mountains and streams, and inquired into the hardship of its restoration: the halls and pavilions were built, but a Chan dwelling was not yet made, and it was still a desolate place. Laici had indeed labored bitterly to protect the Dharma, but the work of carrying it out is the business of our own followers. If the monks do not press forward to do it, they betray the intention of its founding; I fear that if Zibo and Jiguang have spirits, they will not close their eyes. Therefore he earnestly urged and encouraged the assembly, and Jianyin and the monk became its leaders. Hearing this, the monk at once roused an excellent mind, universally converted the great donors, and adorned the Buddha-land; then he shouldered his staff and left the mountain. As he was about to set out he asked for instruction. The Elder, wishing to firm his vow, joyfully taught him, saying:

Though you have left home, you have not yet heard of the practice that transcends the world. Formerly our original teacher Śākyamuni gave up the position of a golden-wheel king, hid his light in the Snow Mountains, and practiced austerities for six years, thereby accomplishing perfect enlightenment and becoming the teacher of gods and humans. In truth, through long distant kalpas he had broadly cultivated merit and wisdom. Hence it is said that in the three-thousand great-thousand world-system there is no place the size of a mustard seed where the bodhisattva did not give up body and life for living beings. As for giving away head, eyes, brains, and marrow as one casts off spittle — this was not for one or two kalpas, but through measureless kalpas, life after life, birth after birth, such bitter practice. Only then did he win a body and land of excellent marks and wondrous adornment. Even the single bowl of rice of a Dharma-ending disciple today was bought with the Tathāgata’s body, life, bones, and blood, and left for his children and grandchildren to enjoy. Seen thus, we who have left home, with clothing and food ready-made and dwelling at ease in comfort — how can we lightly consume it? If one does not think of repaying the Buddha’s kindness, embodying the Buddha’s mind, practicing the Buddha’s practice, and managing the Buddha’s household affairs, then though named a home-leaver, one is in truth provisioning the implements of suffering in the three evil paths. What is meant by embodying the Buddha’s mind? The mind of great compassion. By practicing the Buddha’s practice? The mind of patience and forbearance. By the Buddha’s household affairs? Widely practicing the six pāramitās, accomplishing the two adornments, establishing the Three Jewels, and spreading the transformation of Dharma. If one does not do thus, one is not a disciple of the Buddha but a thief, stealing the Buddha’s robe to nourish the root of one’s own suffering. What benefit is there in leaving home like that? As for the two adornments of merit and wisdom: to resolve to awaken the seed of prajñā, to understand and penetrate one’s own mind and wondrously accord with the Buddha’s mind — this is called wisdom. To broadly practice the pāramitā of giving, adorn the land, and bring living beings to accomplishment — this is called merit. Hence it is said, “Merit and wisdom both complete, one is called the doubly-honored one.” Therefore I now urge the monk, first, to resolve to seek prajñā, to understand and awaken his own mind, and so to escape the bitter sea of birth and death; and second, to broadly practice all practices, universally converting the ten directions and adorning the Buddha-lands, and so to accomplish the pure karma of the Pure Land. Apart from these two practices there is nothing to cultivate. Yet the Buddha said that teaching and converting living beings is precisely adorning the Buddha-land. For the living beings of the great earth are drowned in the bitter sea of greed and desire and all create the bitter karma of birth and death, sunk for long kalpas with no way out of themselves; hence they bring about the implements of suffering of the three realms and three paths. They depend on the Three Jewels as their field of merit, in which to plant the seed of prajñā as the cause and condition of their own enjoyment in other lives. But this must rely on the Jewel of the Saṅgha to open and guide them. Therefore we disciples of the Buddha, if we can convert one person to rouse an excellent mind and break his stinginess and greed, then one person purifies his own mind and adorns one person’s Buddha-land. Convert many, and one adorns many people’s Buddha-lands. If one can convert the whole great earth and make everyone rouse the mind, then one perfects everyone’s Buddha-land. This is to turn a defiled land into a Pure Land and transform implements of suffering into implements of joy — is this not the most excellent and supreme wondrous practice? The monk is going. Take a few words of the Elder and go; then you are a heroic man. At once rouse the vast and great mind. Like the butcher Broad-Brow, who put down his cleaver and straightway did the Buddha’s work; or like the eight-year-old dragon girl who, in the instant of offering her jewel, attained bodhi. There will surely be those who can break the bag of stinginess and give freely even of dung and earth, and so accomplish your vow. Strive, monk — by no means be idle.
