Instructions to the Elder Jianyin Ci of Guizong, Who Went About Begging to Adorn the Buddha-Land

On the summit of the Golden Wheel Peak at Mount Kuang there are the relics of Śākyamuni Tathāgata — a place where the dharma-body ever abides. From of old the Patriarchs established the great banner of Dharma here; thirty-seven came before and after, and how many clarified the mind-ground and transcended birth and death among them is beyond knowing. Know then that the numinosity of this mountain is truly the Jetavana of China and the Vulture Peak of the Western River. As the Dharma’s fortune shifted and declined with the times, the jeweled palaces and Brahma halls fell away into wild thickets. Formerly Master Zibo walked this ground and resolved to restore it. His sincere spirit moved the hidden, and the withered tree flourished again — a strange omen indeed. Thereupon his disciple, the Venerable Fazhan Guo, set his mind on continuing the work and vowed to renew it, his resolve firm and unshakable, like Kang Senghui’s seeking of relics for Jianchu Temple. Before long the present Emperor was moved to bestow the imperial canon to guard the mountain gate; at that time the relics appeared and gave forth great light; mountains and rivers shook and roared, and grasses and trees showed auspicious signs. Truly a rare and excellent event in the Dharma-ending age. In the autumn of the bingchen year the Elder came from Nanyue to pay homage to the Tathāgata’s relics. Gazing up in reliance at the rare and surpassing sight, he was moved to feeling as he looked about. He saw only that the halls and pavilions were adorned but very far from complete; if one faltered midway, it would be no different from the former wild thicket — would that be the meaning of the dragons’ and gods’ protection? The original donor, the layman Xing Laici, has a great vow but weak strength; this is the responsibility of us śramaṇas, sons of Śākyamuni. Therefore he urged the Venerable Jianyin Ci to rouse a vast and great mind and to think how hard such a meeting is to encounter; he should spread his five limbs and give up the four elements to make adornment. Moreover, there are the vow-kings — officials and laymen who long ago received the Buddha’s charge on Vulture Peak — in the ten directions; why not universally invite them to gather and accomplish this excellent work? Then you will not betray the compassionate Father’s entrusting of the family estate to you. Hearing this, the Venerable Ci roused great courage and asked the Elder for a word to serve as his vanguard. The Elder laughed and said: There is no need for that. In the ocean-assembly of the dharma-realm, within the lotus-treasury, the boundless Buddha-lands with their wondrous adornment are all manifested within a single thought of the bodhisattva of the great mind, complete and full, with nothing lacking and nothing left over. It all lies in the power of a single thought of inspired resolve. It is just as the tower of Maitreya contains and holds measureless Buddha-lands, and so Sudhana came before it and did not see it; it required the power of the Great One’s snap of the fingers. Thus the Elder’s words are like one light snap of the fingers before the tower: as for adorning the Buddha-land, if you are but willing to open the door, it appears at once, all at once. What further strength is needed? Go, sir; do not be idle.
Instructions to the Layman Wang Ziju, Who Gave Up His Son to Leave Home

The layman Wang Ziju of Xindu had a son, Yingchen, who in childhood studied the Confucian books. One day he thought that the matter of birth and death is great, roused the mind to leave home, cut off his own hair, and went to Mount Kuang to pay homage to Master Jingtang of Yunzhong. In the summer of the bingchen year I came from Nanyue to this mountain. The layman visited me, and because the deepest affection of kinship is hard to sever, I therefore instructed him, saying: The hope that parents the world over place in a son is that he may bring honor to the name and glory to his parents; hence they take the support of three victims and five cauldrons as the fulfillment of filial piety. They do not realize that the richer the support, the deeper the suffering — it burdens one’s parents and is not true filial piety. Therefore our Buddha, the World-Honored One, thought little of the golden wheel and would not be it; he gave up father and mother, abandoned the royal palace, practiced austerities in the Snow Mountains, and after six years accomplished the Way, becoming the honored one of the three realms, revered by gods and humans. If he had not given up the most precious and cut off the greatest love, how could he have won an undecaying enterprise through long kalpas? Hence he is called “the greatly filial Śākyamuni, the Honored One, who through kalpas repaid his parents’ kindness.” Is this not to take the awakening to the unborn and the universal saving of living beings as the ground of repayment? When the Buddha taught the great precepts, he began with “filial piety is called the precepts” — meaning to be filial to father and mother, filial to teachers, monks, and the Three Jewels, filial to the ultimate Way, filial to all living beings. Therefore one who truly practices the Buddha’s practice will regard all living beings as his parents through many lives — how could he fail to repay the parents of this one life? It is only to be feared that one who leaves home does not know its root. Now if the son takes the resolve to awaken to the unborn as his root and ground, and if he truly settles his will, then not only will repayment be more than enough, but support will also be more than enough. What the world calls filial piety is to use merit and fame to win the support of victims and cauldrons and so please one’s parents. But merit and fame are controlled by the Maker of things, and the victims and cauldrons await what one encounters; to say nothing of the fact that obtaining them multiplies suffering, the whole world seeks them and not all obtain them, and those who obtain them may not be able to enjoy them. There are those who have merit and fame but no emolument; there are parents who cannot wait; and there are those who wait but are not glad — because all depends on fate and not on oneself. But one who has his will set on the great Way seeks within himself, and enjoys within himself too; he holds the strategy of certain attainment and cherishes the support of supreme joy. This cannot be compared with the world. If the layman can give up his son and let him follow his will, then from now on, since the son has hidden his form in the mountain valleys, the layman too may take leave of worldly conditions and follow his son in the mountains. Being able both to cut off love and to transcend the dust, he will have a ground of joy. Then though he wear grass for clothes and eat from trees, brocade and fine fare would be no exchange for it. Father and son, day and night, will think only of the Way; morning consultation and evening inquiry would not be surpassed by a child playing in colored robes to amuse his parents. Water flowing and wind moving, the sound of scripture and the Buddha’s name, are not to be wearied of as loud strings and urgent pipes are. Bright lamps and clear incense, unbroken from dusk to dawn, are not to be compared with the reek of blood and filth. A thousand-fathom cold cliff and a three-room thatched hut make lofty halls and broad mansions look mean indeed. Father and son saving each other and together accomplishing the unsurpassed Way, enjoying honor and fame not of this world — this is a thing that must be attained. Compared with the grant of one office and the praise of one word, which cannot be counted on, it is as different as cloud from mud, heaven from earth. What the layman gives up is small, and what he wins is great; what the son goes against is slight, and what he accords with is deep. Is this not the great filial piety of the world? The layman joyfully received the teaching and asked for a name, wishing to hold to it as a disciple. The Elder named him Fuzhi — “blessing arrives” — meaning that his blessing comes from now on. His style he named Dalai — “the great comes” — meaning that what is given up is small and what comes is great. So he wrote this as a document of the Dharma gate for the son.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Lingyuan Jue

The Chan monk had dwelt at Guizong on Mount Lu for years. He said he knew his faculties were inferior and that he could not enter at one leap, so he had made a vow to recite the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma ten thousand times in this life, and he asked for confirmation. He did not know whether this practice was the same as or different from the work of investigation, and wished to hear instruction. The Elder therefore taught him, saying: The Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma is like eating honey: the middle and the edges are both sweet, fundamentally without difference of taking and rejecting. It is only because students rejoice in one thing and weary of another that differences arise. Therefore our Buddha came into the world expressly to open and show living beings the one great matter and its causes and conditions; and the Patriarch came from the west, pointing directly and transmitting singly, only to make people understand and awaken to this one great matter. What is called the one great matter is precisely the self-mind that living beings originally possess, named the seed of Buddha-nature. Know then that the scriptures are the road the Buddha opened and showed, and Chan is the wish that people walk along the road. To hold the scriptures without awakening the mind, and to investigate Chan without seeing the nature — neither is true practice. The Sixth Patriarch said: “When the mind is deluded, the Lotus turns the mind; when the mind is awakened, the mind turns the Lotus.” How could holding the scripture and investigating Chan be two? It lies in the student’s firm and long-unshakable resolve. Holding the scripture is investigation; investigation is holding the scripture. Therefore the Buddha’s meaning in the scripture, when he sought people in the final age to hold the scripture — was he seeking those who follow the lines and count the ink? The ancients’ investigation required the bitter heart of thirty years. Now ten thousand recitations of the scripture cannot be done in less than thirty years. If the monk can hold this single thought of thirty years of dwelling in the mountain without change, the Buddhas and Patriarchs will surely stroke his head and comfort him. Only discern a willing mind, and you will certainly not be cheated. On no account understand it as two dharmas.
Instructions to the Venerable Chang of Guizong, of the Zongyuan Hermitage in Qiyang

The Venerable Chang had his will set on the matter that goes upward and devoted himself to holding the Lotus Sutra. Hearing that the Elder had come to Mount Kuang, he crawled on hands and knees to see him at Donglin, and told him that in reciting the Lotus Sutra he doubted the passage, “In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle Dharma; apart from the Buddha’s skillful means, they are but provisional names to guide living beings.” He did not know what the One Vehicle is, or what skillful means and provisional names are, and asked for instruction. The Elder said to him: What is called the One Vehicle is the original mind of all living beings — the self-nature of awareness that is present before us in daily use. Because this mind-nature is the great root of all sages and ordinary beings, it is called a vehicle; vehicle means that which carries. Hence it is said, “The dharmas above and below in the three realms are made by one mind alone.” Outside this mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable. Even in our daily use, at the gates of the six faculties, seeing and hearing without delusion, clearly and constantly knowing, not obscured by the dust of toil and deluded thought, the light shines universally and the numinous awareness is luminous — this one mind is the realm of the Buddha, and so it carries one to Buddhahood. If with this mind one broadly practices the six pāramitās and gathers and converts living beings, without seeing any living being to save or any Buddha to attain, then this one mind is the realm of the bodhisattva, and it carries one to bodhisattvahood. If with this mind one contemplates the four noble truths, can cut off the cause of suffering, craving, and affliction, transcend the three realms, and realize the joy of cessation, then this is the realm of the two vehicles, and it carries one to the two vehicles. If with this mind one diligently cultivates the pure life, the four dhyānas and eight concentrations, then it is the realm of the four holy ones and four dhyānas, and it carries one to the Brahma heavens. If one can cultivate the ten good deeds and cut off the highest grade of evil, one is moved to the realm of the heavens of the six desires, and it carries one to the heavens. If one is deluded about this one mind and gives free rein to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, cutting off the Buddha-seed nature, one is moved to the harsh retribution of the three paths, and it carries one into the three evil destinies. Therefore the Buddha said the three realms are mind only; apart from this one mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable. This one matter alone, and no other matter — therefore it is called the One Vehicle. It is not that apart from this mind there is another dharma to speak of. If there were a dharma outside the mind, that would be the false view of the outsiders, not right Dharma. If one understands this mind, then one knows that the three worthy ones and ten sages, and all living beings, are but shadows and echoes of the one mind, and that the Way is a provisional name. Then one knows that the three vehicles and twelve divisions of the teaching spoken by the Buddha are arranged according to capacity and are all provisional names to guide living beings; there was originally no real dharma to give people. All the various skillful means were for opening and showing this mind, not that there is another, different dharma taught to living beings. Not only is the Buddha’s teaching a skillful means; even the final twirling of the flower and Kāśyapa’s smile, and Bodhidharma’s coming from the west to transmit singly the mind-seal, are also skillful means. As for what is called “pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha” — to say “pointing directly” is already crooked. Students in the final age do not understand their own mind but seek only outside, and in the end have utterly no true benefit. And if they have the will to investigate the matter that goes upward, they do not know that fundamentally there is no dharma, and do not understand that their own mind is one flavor of reality, but want to seek the wondrous elsewhere. Applying the mind thus, not only is the true eye unclear, but they fall into the false views of the outsiders; though named students of the Way, they unknowingly become seeds of hell. Is this not pitiable? The Elder has often said that a student should above all apply his mind truly, and purify his own afflictions and habits and the seeds of karmic consciousness. Break one part of karmic consciousness, and one part of the Buddha’s knowing and seeing is exposed; understand one part of the Buddha’s realm. Cut off ten parts of karmic consciousness, and it is ten parts of the Buddha’s realm. How could there be a clever method outside the mind, patched together and brought in, that could be the Buddha’s realm? Chan monk, doubt no more. Simply understand that your own mind is the One Vehicle; if you awaken to the fact that all dharmas are but provisional names, that is true work. You must simply, in all places, not be deluded. Put your strength into the work thus, and do not make another kind of calculation and reckoning — all of that is the seed of false views.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Guyu Zhuo

The Chan monk Guyu came from Fuliang to consult at the Golden Wheel and asked for instruction on doing the work. The Elder asked him: How do you apply your mind in daily use? He answered: I contemplate that all is mind only. The Elder asked again: When you contemplate thus, do you still see objects? He answered: At this point I see no objects at all. The Elder said: Since you see no objects, what is it that is mind only? The monk said: I simply do not forget the subject. The Elder said: You say “mind only,” but you are doing the work with knowing and seeing; in truth you have not understood the state of mind only. The ancient worthy said: “Not yet understanding that objects are mind only, one gives rise to all kinds of discrimination; having understood that objects are mind only, discrimination no longer arises.” Do you still give rise to discrimination toward the objects before you? If when you contemplate you seem to forget objects, yet when you meet conditions you discriminate as before and give rise to mind in pursuit of objects, then to insist on saying “mind only” like this will in the end never yield real proof. Even if you can forget the objects before you, if you cling to “mind only,” then you cannot forget the mind; you have forgotten the object but not the subject. Therefore mind and objects cannot merge and fuse, and this is called the obstruction of wisdom. How much less, when you have not even forgotten objects, to insist on “mind only” and take it as a real dharma? The ancient worthy said: “If a hair’s breadth is not penetrated, it is as though a thousand mountains stood between.” Even if you reach the point where mind and objects are both forgotten and not a single dharma is established, that is still a matter on the edge of knowing and seeing — how much more to take the thinking mind as the ultimate? Is that not deceiving oneself? The monk is now going to the depths of the ten thousand peaks of Nanyue. Earnestly observe the water flowing and wind moving, birdsong and mountain light — filling the eyes and ears, utterly without the marks of body, mind, or world, beaten into one piece. Even these two words “mind only” must be thrown beyond the ten thousand worlds; there is something further. If you fall into the nest of “mind only,” you will still have no share in getting out.
Instructions to Yuan Gongliao

The Buddha said that even the wriggling and the sentient all have Buddha-nature; the tradition says that a person can be a Yao or a Shun. From this we know that the nature of numinous awareness is the root of things, and that there is no one who does not possess it. Yet observing the people born through past and present, heroes are not few, while sages and worthies are not commonly seen. Why? Because of the bias of habitual defilement: people follow feeling and chase after things without turning back. This is what is meant by “the common people use it daily and do not know it.” If one can seek to know oneself, then sagehood is not hard. Hence it is said, “One who knows himself is clear.” Because one does not know oneself, delusion daily thickens and the mind daily darkens. If there is a heroic person who blocks feeling and restores the nature, then sagehood may be expected, and his enterprise will surely be undecaying. The Buddha’s ten precepts, Confucius’s four noes, and Chan’s one mind are all essentials of restoring the nature. A person of will — can he not strive? Yuanzi Daosheng, now called Suling, once came to inquire of me at Caoxi, and I knew him to be a vessel of the sharpest faculties. When I passed Mount Kuang, he waited for me from afar; seeing what he had composed, his bones were extraordinary and his nature quick. But his habits are heavy and his temper high, and so he gives free rein to habit without seeing the nature. If he can strive to keep feeling at a distance and restore the nature, then he will not be proud, not contrary, not niggardly, not bent on success; then his vessel will be broad without overflowing, his will firm and unmoved, his mind cool and his temper dissolved, and he may sit and advance in this Way. Sagehood may be expected — how much more so worldly achievement? The Elder loved him and taught him the method of investigating the mind, much like the worn shoe on the bridge of Yishui. So he named him Gongliao, hoping that he would daily grow more indifferent to what is sweet to the palate.
Essentials of Chan Investigation (An Informal Instruction in the Chan Hall at Mount Jing)

The Chan school is one lineage, for transmitting the Buddha’s mind-seal; it is fundamentally no small matter. From Bodhidharma’s coming from the west, the purport of single transmission was established, using the four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra to seal the mind. Thus although Chan is a special transmission outside the teachings, in truth it uses the teachings for verification, and only then is the Buddha’s and Patriarchs’ non-dual Way seen. Its work of investigation also comes from the teachings. The Laṅkāvatāra says: “Sitting quietly in mountain forests, cultivating the upper, middle, and lower, one can see the surging flow of one’s own deluded thoughts.” This is truly the World-Honored One’s precise instruction on the method of doing the work. It also says: “Mind, consciousness, and mentation are manifested by one’s own mind; the states of self-nature are marks of the false. The ocean of birth and death, karma, craving, and not-knowing — all such causes are transcended.” This is the Tathāgata’s precise instruction on the wondrous purport of awakening the mind. It also says: “The holy ones of the lineage transmitted it one to another: deluded thought has no nature.” This again is the precise instruction of the secret mind-seal. This is the essential place where the yellow-faced old fellow taught people to investigate. And when Bodhidharma instructed the Second Patriarch he said: “Simply let outer conditions rest, and within have no panting; make the mind like a wall, and you may enter the Way.” This is the essential method by which Bodhidharma first taught people to investigate. When it was transmitted to Huangmei and the time came to seek an heir, the Sixth Patriarch simply said, “From the first not a single thing exists,” and received the robe and bowl. This is the precise purport of the transmitted mind-seal. And when the Sixth Patriarch returned south and instructed Daoming, saying, “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — at that very moment, what is the Original Face of the Venerable Ming?” — this is the Sixth Patriarch’s first precise formula for teaching people to investigate. Know then that the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the lineage only taught people to understand and awaken to their own mind and to recognize themselves; there was never any talk of public cases and huatous. From Nanyue and Qingyuan onward, the Patriarchs instructed as was fitting, mostly striking at the place of doubt, so that people would turn head and brain around and stop. Even for those who did not understand, though he applied the hammer and tongs, he simply left it to their time and conditions. It was Huangbo who first taught people to look into a huatou; and only with Chan Master Dahui was it strongly advocated, teaching students to investigate one public case of the ancients as a nose-hold, calling it a huatou, and requiring people to hold it up earnestly. Why? Only because in the field of the eighth consciousness of students the seeds of bad habit from measureless kalpas inwardly perfume, surging on in continuous succession, deluded thoughts unbroken, and there is no help for it. So he gave you a meaningless phrase to bite firmly on, first putting down all inner and outer mind-object deluded thoughts at once. And because you cannot put them down, he taught you to raise this huatou, like cutting a tangled skein of silk: one cut, and all is cut, no longer continuing. Block the consciousness and do not let it pass again. This is precisely Bodhidharma’s rule of “outer conditions resting, within no panting, mind like a wall.” Without taking it in hand thus, you will never see your own Original Face. It is not teaching you to ponder over the words of a public case and make them into a doubt, hoping to get an explanation from them. Even Dahui, who taught only looking into the huatou and used a poisoned hand, wanted only for you to kill the thieving mind. As he said in instructing the assembly: “In investigating Chan you need only empty the mind. Paste the two words ‘birth and death’ on your forehead, like a man who owes another ten thousand strings of cash. Three times by day, three times by night, in tea and in rice, walking and standing, sitting and lying, when exchanging courtesies with friends, in quiet and in noise, raise a huatou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature?’ Zhou answered, ‘No.’ Just look at it this way and that within; when it has no flavor it is like butting against a wall; when you come to the crucial juncture it is like a mouse entering a horn — and then you will see it cut off.” He wanted you to prepare a long-range body and mind and wrestle with it; then suddenly the flower of mind will bloom, illumining the lands of the ten directions, and one awakening will be thorough. These are the tongs and hammers that Elder Dahui customarily used. His meaning was only that you should use the huatou to block and intercept the deluded thoughts beneath the faculty of mind, so that their surging cannot proceed; and right at the place where they do not proceed, look into and take up your Original Face. He was not teaching you to ponder over a public case, to make it a doubt, and to seek an explanation. As he said, “How could the blooming of the mind-flower be gotten from another?” As the Buddhas and Patriarchs above have each pointed out, they want you to investigate yourself, not to seek from their mysterious and wondrous phrases. People today who investigate Chan and do the work all say they look into a huatou and bring down doubt, but they do not know to investigate at the root; they only seek on the huatou itself. Seeking and seeking, suddenly they think up a stretch of scenery and say they are awakened; then they compose verses and present odes, take it as rare goods, and think they have got it — never knowing that they have fallen wholly into the net of deluded knowing and seeing. Is not investigating Chan like this blinding the eyes of the people of the whole world for generations to come? Young people today, before their sitting cushion is steady, claim to have awakened to the Way, then show off their mouths, play with their spirits, and take it for the swiftness of the Chan mechanism; they think up a few groundless, wild, random words and call them verses on the ancients. That comes from your own deluded thought — when did you ever dream of the ancients being present? If awakening to the Way today were so easy, then the ancients’ practice — like Changqing, who sat through and wore out seven cushions; like Zhaozhou, who for thirty years did not mix his mind with anything else — by this comparison the ancients were the dullest-facultied people and would be of no use to you moderns even to carry your straw sandals. The person of overweening pride, who has not attained and says he has attained — should one not fear this? As for investigating Chan, looking into the huatou, and bringing down doubt — these can never be dispensed with. What is called “small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening; no doubt, no awakening.” One must simply be good at using doubt. If the doubt is broken, then the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ nostrils are naturally strung through on one thread. Take the public case of looking into the Buddha-recitation: just examine earnestly who it is that recites the Buddha’s name; do not doubt who the Buddha is. If you doubt who the Buddha is, you need only listen to the lecturer explain that Amitābha Buddha is named Infinite Light, and you would then be awakened, and compose a few verses on Infinite Light. If this were called awakening to the Way, then those who awaken to the mind would be as many as hemp and millet. Bitter, bitter! The ancients said a huatou is like a tile for knocking on a door: you only knock the door open to see the person inside; you do not do your business outside the door. This is enough to show that when doubt is raised from the huatou, the doubt is not on the huatou but must be at the root. Take Jiashan’s consultation with Chuanzi: he asked, “A line cast a thousand feet down, the intent is in the deep pool. Three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him with the oar and knocked him into the water. When Jiashan had climbed back into the boat, the Master said again, “Speak! Speak!” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him again, and Jiashan was greatly awakened and nodded three times. The Master said: “The line at the pole’s end is yours to play with; not stirring the clear waves, your intent is of itself distinct.” If Jiashan had been doing his business on the hook and line, how could Chuanzi have given his life to get him through? This is the ancients’ quick and easy, skillful way of getting out. In the past, when the Chan way flourished, there were clear-eyed teachers everywhere, and students of investigation were many throughout the world, and everywhere there was opening and unfolding. Hence it was said, “It is not that there is no Chan; it is only that there are no teachers.” Now the Chan school has been silent for a long time. How fortunate that at one time many have roused the mind to investigate. Yet though there are teachers, some measure the capacity and weigh the advance, and verify according to feeling; the student’s mind is shallow and he thinks he has got it. He does not believe the Tathāgata’s holy teaching, does not seek the true road, but only does his work muddle-headedly, and then takes a winter-melon seal as the final decision. He not only deceives himself but deceives others as well — should one not fear this? Take the officials and laymen of old who were recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp: there were only a few. People amid the toil of the dust today do not cultivate even the coarse precepts; their turbid deluded thoughts run wild; relying on their own cleverness and having read a few karmic encounters of the ancient worthies, each one is self-conceited as a person of the highest faculties; seeing a monk, they at once contest Chan repartee, and also take themselves to be awakened to the Way. This, though a fault of the times, is truly a case of us followers, one blind man leading a crowd of blind men. The Elder now follows the true and essential place of the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ work and discusses it with you all. Those of high clarity and understanding will have their own way to correct it.
Instructions to Dong Zhiguang

The student Dong Sizhang grew up in a house of wealth and honor, and early roused the mind to seek escape from birth and death — surely the power of the inward perfuming of a surpassing affinity with prajñā planted in former lives. He first consulted Master Yunqi, who taught him the Dharma gate of the Pure Land. Then he consulted the Elder at Shuangjing and wished to receive the upāsaka precepts. He also of himself exposed his deep and heavy karmic offenses and asked for the essentials of escaping suffering, and by what cultivation he might extinguish his offenses. The Elder therefore taught him, saying: Since a student knows the root of his offenses is deep and heavy, the ancient worthies taught people to dissolve old karma as it comes and never to create new calamity. For living beings heavy in karma the Buddha opened the one gate of repentance, which is the most skillful means of escaping suffering. The verse says: “All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them. If one wishes to repent, let him sit upright and contemplate true reality.” This is the correct practice; all else is auxiliary skillful means. The self-nature of living beings is equal to the Buddha’s, originally undefiled and without the marks of birth and death, coming and going. But because of the first non-awakening one is deluded about one’s own nature, and so it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, deluded thoughts arise, all kinds of inversion, and one creates all kinds of karma, falsely taking the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not understanding one’s own mind, one is turned about by deluded thought. It is like a person fast asleep who has all kinds of evil dreams, all kinds of states, all kinds of terror, unbearable suffering — and when he wakes he seeks the things of the dream and cannot find them at all. Thus living beings fall into the dream of ignorance, follow deluded inversion, create all kinds of karma, and take on all kinds of suffering for themselves. Seen with waking eyes, how could all those inverted conditions be found? But now, within the dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve old karma? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and truly believe that one’s own mind is originally pure, not driven by deluded inversion. Then karma has no cause — for deluded thought is the cause of all karma. Why? Because from beginningless time one has been deluded about one’s own original mind, and life after life has created all kinds of karma with a deluded mind; the habit of karma accumulates within the field of the eighth consciousness and is watered by the water of ignorance, so that these evil seeds sprout the shoots of karma — this is the root of offenses. All evil karma arises from this. If you now wish to dissolve old karma, you must first rouse the great light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and not allow deluded thoughts to sprout and secretly grow. If you can cut off with a single thought the place where deluded thought arises, then the root of accumulated karma is dissolved on the spot. What is called “I do not fear the arising of a thought; I fear only that awareness is late.” If awareness and illumination are even slightly late, you will be turned about by it. If in daily use, at the place where mind stirs and thoughts arise, you are aware thought after thought and extinguish them thought after thought, this is what is meant by “all offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them.” For the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom — this is what is meant by wisdom being able to dissolve them. If day and night without cease you diligently observe and do not let it pass, but simply at the place where deluded thought arises investigate it to the point of utterly no mark of arising, looking and looking and in the end finding nothing obtainable — then after a long time, when it is pure and familiar, your own mind will be pure and without a thing. A mind without things is true reality. If you constantly contemplate this mind, what deluded thought can lodge in it, what accumulated karma can rest on it? Applying the mind thus is called the samādhi of contemplation. If your own afflictions are coarse and heavy and you are not aware at the place where ignorance obstructs, then the ancient worthies had people investigate: take the public case of examining the Buddha-recitation and put your strength right there. Raise one recitation of the Buddha’s name and lay it across your breast; then examine just who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. Thus as you raise it, so you examine it, never letting it go empty. Lay this mass of doubt across your breast like your own root of life, never letting it go. In all movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, coming and going, sitting and standing, this one matter alone, and no other. Applying the mind thus, as soon as you see a deluded thought arise, give the huatou one thrust, and it shatters on the spot; all deluded thoughts naturally vanish without trace. With this huatou, like the sun’s disk in the sky, there is no darkness it does not illumine. I fear only that the mind’s strength is lazy and you will not earnestly hold it up, and so cannot match the deluded thoughts. If you can match them, then the place where deluded thoughts dissolve is the time when old karma dissolves. Apart from this one point, to seek elsewhere outside the mind means that even were the Buddhas to appear in the world there would be no place for repentance. This lies in one’s own power; no other power can substitute for it. If bad habits are strong and your strength cannot match them, then in the past the Buddha gave clear instruction: if a practitioner’s habits are not removed, he should single-mindedly recite the mind-mantra spoken by me, the unconditioned Mind-Buddha. This is truly an extraordinary skillful means. Because each person’s storehouse consciousness flows secretly and his habits are deep and thick, and the power of wisdom does not reach there — at the place it cannot reach, one must rely on the Buddha’s mind-seal to break it secretly. It is like a hard-to-break rebel: one must request the sword from above. This requires that morning and evening you find your own skillful means. But take the work of investigation as the highest principle. The Elder instructs you thus, much like giving a blind man a staff. In truth, the practice lies with oneself; neither teacher nor friend can substitute. Because the layman’s will is set on the Dharma gate, he is named Fujue, “blessing-awakening,” taking awareness and illumination as the root of practice. His style is Zhiguang, “wisdom-light” — for without the light of wisdom, how could one break the darkness of delusion? Only you must let awareness and illumination be undimmed and the light of wisdom be present before you; then that is the time of ending karmic obstruction and escaping birth and death.
Instructions to Wen Rudong

The layman Vimalakīrti dwelt at home in the city of Vaiśālī, swept away all he owned, and lived alone in a single room, using illness as a way to teach the Dharma. Even Mañjuśrī and the thirty-two great ones exhausted their eloquence and could not match his one silent word. He is the first of all laypeople since ancient times to do the Buddha’s work well. Old Pang dispersed all his family wealth, received from Mazu the great meaning of the coming from the west, and said, “I only wish to empty what exists; never make real what does not.” He again is one who learned well from Vimalakīrti. Layman Rudong, take these two elders as your good teachers.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Huanyou Hai, Hall Master of Mount Jing

The Buddhas and Patriarchs are one mind; the teachings and Chan are one. The Chan school’s special transmission outside the teachings is not that apart from the mind there is another dharma to transmit; it only wants people to leave behind language and writing and awaken singly to the purport beyond words. Chan practitioners today at once disparage the teachings, not knowing that the teachings expound one mind, which is the root of Chan. But the Buddha’s exposition of one mind covers both the deluded and the awakened paths thoroughly; the Chan school points directly at one mind, which does not belong to delusion or awakening, and wants people to awaken thoroughly. In truth, ultimately there is no two. In the Tathāgata-garbha, coming and going, delusion and awakening, birth and death are utterly unobtainable — how could this belong to delusion and awakening? The Second Patriarch said, “Seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable.” The Sixth Patriarch said, “From the first not a single thing exists.” This is precisely prajñā without the five aggregates, faculties, dust, and consciousness-realms, and without the dharmas of the three vehicles that transcend the world. “Because there is nothing to be obtained, one obtains bodhi” and “seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable” — how are these two dharmas? Know then that the teaching’s exposition of one mind has only a surplus of ordinary feeling and sagely understanding. Chan investigation suddenly breaks ignorance — that is cutting off ordinary feeling. Even awakening is spat out — that is cutting off sagely understanding. Thus Chan rebukes knowing and understanding, and the teachings were never not rebuking it either. Those who today turn from the teachings to Chan but cannot forget knowing and cut off understanding, who take up the huatou but cannot forget feeling and cut off traces, are all rebuked. How can one slander the teachings and say they are not worth taking? Those who today abandon the teachings to investigate Chan: if they can first understand that fundamentally there is no ordinary being or sage and that it does not belong to delusion or awakening, that is their ground of view. Investigating according to this, if in one’s thought there remains the slightest feeling-view or wondrous knowing and understanding, it is all not yet penetrated and is a matter on the edge of birth and death — how can one take it as attainment? Today, with no clear-eyed teacher to verify, if one does not use the teachings to seal the mind, one will end in the false paths of demons and outsiders. But one must not take the Buddha’s spoken words and the Patriarchs’ wondrous phrases as one’s own knowing and seeing; one must investigate until one reaches the place of accord. As the scripture says, “All afflictions should, at a thought, be transformed into unsurpassed awareness.” This is what sudden awakening looks like. One must not mix afflictions and habits with knowing and seeing and take that as wondrous awakening. Nor is it anything separate in addition: it is only the dissolving of afflictions and habits and the exposing of the Original Face. Hence it is said, “After awakening, one is the same as before awakening; still simply the person of former times, not changing the place of former practice.” Have you not heard how Jiashan, before he met Chuanzi, entered the hall and a monk asked him, “What is the dharma-body?” Shan said, “The dharma-body is without marks.” He also asked, “What is the dharma-eye?” Shan said, “The dharma-eye is without blemish.” Daowu was sitting there and could not help laughing. After he had met Chuanzi, Daowu sent a monk to ask, “What is the dharma-body?” Shan still said, “The dharma-body is without marks.” He asked again, “What is the dharma-eye?” Shan still said, “The dharma-eye is without blemish.” The monk returned and reported this to Daowu. Daowu said, “This fellow has finally penetrated.” This is the model of a clever lecturer who abandons the teachings to investigate Chan. Hall Master Hai has long been intimate with the teachings; now he abandons what he has studied and seeks only the road that goes upward. Look at how Jiashan’s two turning words before and after are the same — why did Daowu approve the latter and not the former? Try to see where he did not approve and where he approved. If here you can settle it, I guarantee you will spit out the meaning of the teachings and the meaning of the Patriarchs all at once. Another day you will be able to drink up the whole canon in one gulp, and every word will turn into a treasury of light. Enough of these tangled vines. Take care, take care.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Lingjian Zhi, of the West Hall at Mount Jing

The teachings say: “All dharmas are unborn; I speak of the meaning of the instant. At the very moment of arising there is ceasing; this is not spoken for the foolish.” The ancient worthy said, “One who awakens to the unborn first sees the instant.” But having awakened to the unborn, what instant is there to see? If one sees an instant, then one has not awakened to the unborn. Now why is it said that one who awakens to the unborn first sees the instant? Then are the unborn and the instant one or different? The Buddha spoke of the instant in reliance on the unborn, so they are not different. The Patriarch said, “One who awakens to the unborn first sees the instant” — so the unborn and the instant are again not one. If one seeks it apart from oneness and difference, then the meaning of the unborn becomes a stake to tether a donkey. Weishan said: “People today who in one thought suddenly understand their own mind are said to be awakened. Then, with that which they have awakened to, they purify the present karma and its flowing consciousness — this is called cultivation.” Now the flowing consciousness means the subtle arising and ceasing, which is the mind of the instant. To speak of cultivating after awakening means that one sees it after awakening. And if one sees the instant only after awakening, then the earlier awakening was clearly not true unborn. Today, in Chan investigation one raises a huatou, and though this is called putting forth effort, the subtle arising and ceasing flows on secretly, like a stone pressing grass: it darkens and is not seen. If one does not cut off arising and ceasing, how can one awaken to the unborn? And if it is not the unborn, how can one match birth and death? If one sees it only after awakening, then the World-Honored One’s speaking of the unborn in reliance on the instant becomes a superfluous dharma. The West Hall master has eaten his fill of the teachings; now he abandons what he has studied and takes up the single road that goes upward. Settle this for yourself here. But you must not reconcile it by doctrine and principle, nor seek it in intellectual understanding. If you can, within the instant of a single thought, suddenly see the unborn, then the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ nostrils are strung through on one thread.
Instructions to the Hermitage Master Zhixi Xian

The hermitage master had long dwelt in the lecture halls, and then practiced with the Patriarchs’ karmic encounters at Shaolin. Now he has swept aside all he had studied and takes up the single road that goes upward, hanging his shadow at Shuangjing. Just then the Elder arrived, and he offered incense and asked for instruction. The Elder taught him, saying: In this matter everyone is originally without deficiency, complete and full. The reason they do not know it in daily use and gain no benefit from it is simply that the seeds of beginningless bad habit have been perfumed and dyed deep through accumulated kalpas and are already hard to pull out; and now they are newly perfumed with the words of the teachings, the Patriarchs’ public cases, and all kinds of knowing and seeing, adding another layer of obstruction. Though one wants to understand oneself, the more one seeks the farther away it goes. Why? Only because one is blind to oneself and seeks it from others. The afflictions and habits accumulated over lives are called the obstruction of affliction; the wondrous knowing and seeing are called the obstruction of the known. If the two obstructions are dissolved, the original substance appears of itself. In investigating the matter that goes upward today, one must first spit out utterly all the words and languages and wondrous principles one has learned before, naming them mixed poison. Take up the root huatou alone and bring down the doubt again; cut off the root of deluded thought and affliction, so that inwardly it cannot get out and outwardly cannot get in. With the former and latter limits cut, what lies between is naturally alone. Only one mass of doubt, as your own root of life. Doubt until you cannot doubt and cannot exert effort; then fix your gaze upon it and see what on earth it is. Look and look, press and press, and there will come a time of cutting off. But if the least knowing and seeing remains, then a thousand or ten thousand li lie between. Just look at the First Patriarch’s saying, “Make the mind like a wall, and you may enter the Way.” This is the first road home. If the mind will not die and the doubt is not keen, then for a thousand lives and a hundred kalpas you will remain on the road. Hermitage master, simply gather your spirit into this. I guarantee that the place you attain another day will certainly not be reached by “thus, verily, and the like.” Strive greatly.
Instructions to the Hermitage Master Songpu En

The ancient worthies taught people investigating Chan to first shed body and mind inwardly and leave the world behind outwardly, putting everything down and keeping not the slightest trace, and then to take up singly one public case as a huatou — such as Zhaozhou’s “Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhou answered, No”; or “The ten thousand dharmas return to the one; where does the one return to?”; or examining earnestly who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. Raise whichever one and lay it across your breast like a diamond king’s precious sword, cutting off all thoughts and deluded imaginings at once, like cutting a tangled skein of silk. Inwardly it cannot get out, outwardly it cannot get in; block the vital pass and seal the throat, allowing no breath to pass. Press hard thus, and fix your gaze: what on earth is this that takes up the huatou? Bring down doubt thus; doubt on and on, doubt until the mind is like a wall, and never allow a second thought to arise. As soon as a deluded thought secretly flows, see it at a glance, then at once raise the huatou with all your strength and bring down the doubt again; examine and doubt again, and press and block this mass of doubt. When thought does not arise and deluded thinking does not proceed, that is precisely the place of power. Lean steadily on it thus; in all walking, standing, sitting, and lying, amid movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, clench your teeth and resolve never to let it go. Even in dreams do not let it go. There is only the one thought of the huatou, which is the root of life of the person concerned — like a man dead though still breathing. Only by wrestling with a poisoned hand thus is one a person who works at Chan investigation. When your effort reaches its extreme, not counting days and months, suddenly the cold ashes will burst with a bean — that is the time of great joy. If you drift along as you please and work one day and freeze ten, I fear there will never be a time of power. Hermitage master, since you have your will set on the matter that goes upward, encourage yourself with this.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Chengmi Xian

In daily use a student contemplates the four great elements as a shadow, contemplates what is before him as a dream, contemplates the mind as a rushing torrent, contemplates movement as a mechanical puppet, contemplates sounds as echoes in a valley, contemplates objects as flowers in the sky. Contemplating thus, there is no self and no mine; nothing moves me, nothing acts. Coming and going, sitting and standing, there is no arising and no stopping; responding to thought, there is no birth. This is called entering the samādhi of non-contention.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Tanyan Zong

The Chan monk Zong in his youth frequented the lecture halls and habituated himself to the meaning of nature and characteristics. After a long time, because he had not seen his own nature, he roused doubt and investigated. One day, having gained no entry, he met the Elder when he came to Shuangjing, and offered incense to ask for instruction. So the Elder taught him, saying: The ancients said, “I do not value your practice; I value only your ground of view.” What is called practice is the work of advancing; what is called the ground of view is understanding and penetrating one’s own mind as the root of practice. If the root of practice is unclear, then one’s advance loses its aim. Therefore a student of investigation takes the ground of view first. What is called the ground of view is truly believing that one’s own mind is originally pure and utterly without a single thing, and that not only ordinary feeling but even sagehood is not established. It is only because of beginningless ignorance that one obscures one’s own wondrous clarity, and so gives rise to all kinds of inversion and deluded discrimination and creates all kinds of karma. It is like a waking man with nothing to do who suddenly, in sleep, has all kinds of dreams; the sufferings and joys of the dream appear plainly before him, and when he wakes and seeks them they are utterly unobtainable. This is called producing something from nothing — how could it be a real dharma? But the foolish, being inverted, cling to it as truly existing; this is not seeing thoroughly. When the Buddha appeared in the world and taught all kinds of dharmas, these were tools for breaking the dream, and had no root either. And students of the Buddha-Dharma again cling to them as real dharmas of their own — this is adding a dream within a dream. The method of Chan investigation today has no other wondrous formula: it is simply to break the dream-thoughts and inversion. If one understands that fundamentally there is nothing, and truly believes that one’s own mind is pure and without a thing, then one understands that deluded thought does not exist. Understanding that delusion does not exist, one knows that the Buddha-Dharma that breaks deluded thought is also fundamentally nonexistent. Buddha-Dharma is medicine; deluded thought is the disease. If medicine and disease are both not established, then the original substance is at peace. Understanding thus, one knows that both medicine and disease are diseases. The wordless public case of the ancients that one now takes up in investigation is the medicine for attacking the disease of medicine and disease. It is called using poison to remove poison. If one knows that fundamentally there is nothing, then the single word “investigate” is yet another poison laid down. How can one take this as something wondrous? If one does not believe one’s own mind, then even investigating is taking poison by mistake. Can the Chan monk believe this? You should investigate at the place where not a single dharma is established.
Instructions to Gu Shanzi

I was dwelling at Jizhao in Shuangjing when the layman Gu Shanzi came to consult me. I asked his profession; he said he practiced geomancy. Then he came to Huacheng, and because I pointed out the mountains and waters and spoke of the subtlety of the Maker’s transformations, which surpass form and energy, he grasped the essence and let go the coarse. I then questioned him, saying that I had once seen a piece called On Awakening, which my student Zhouzi had written and for which I had written a preface, saying: The One is the root of the ten thousand things, the storehouse of the Maker’s transformations. Hence it is said, “Heaven obtains the One and is clear; earth obtains the One and is at peace; the sage obtains the One and becomes the rectifier of the world.” When rectified, one does not slip into the crooked, and one firms one’s root. Now man and things, principle and energy, mind and form, are all one. Obtain the One, and all principles return to it. The saying goes, “Know the One, and the ten thousand affairs are finished.” Therefore we who investigate the wondrous always say, “The ten thousand dharmas return to the One; where does the One return to?” That the ten thousand return to the One can be known; where the One returns to cannot be known. Now man is bound by the entanglement of ten thousand affairs, and ten thousand cares assault his mind, a welter and a confusion, and in the end he is not at peace — this is the fault of not knowing the One. The layman can observe that heaven and earth and the Maker’s transformations return to the One, yet does not know that body and mind, nature and life, return to the One; this is to know two fives and not to know ten. If one knows that nature and life return to the One, then the ten thousand transformations are complete within me. Can one not attend to this?
Instructions to Tan Liangsheng

Tan Liangsheng’s faculties are the sharpest, for he comes from the habitual practice of prajñā in former lives. Yet prajñā is the Buddha-nature of living beings, complete in each one; that faculties differ as sharp or dull is simply because the habits of the five desires are thick or thin in unequal measure. The sharp-facultied, having long practiced prajñā and purified the habits of defilement, come to this life clever and bright. But people do not know to turn back; they use their sharp faculties and cleverness as provisions for defiled bad habits — this is called inversion. Because prajñā inwardly perfumes them, they now and then have the will to leave the dust, and they say, “At such and such a time, when worldly affairs are finished, I will go and study the Way.” Such a view is common to the whole world. Because they have the thought of a future, whatever conditions they meet before them, since they cherish a lofty ambition for the future, they regard as not worth doing and do not deign to do. By this empty imagining they instead increase their pride and arrogance, thinking that others do not have this mind and are all mediocre. And they themselves let the present pass by, so that both the worldly and the world-transcending are lost, and the light of time is spent in vain; and when the future comes, it may not be as their first resolve wished. Moreover their minds do not check their conduct in small matters, and their feelings remain rough; they take the view of self as high clarity — this is an even greater mistake. To call this having aspiration is rather not as good as the old farmer in a hamlet of three households: he has no other thoughts, and year after year his livelihood is not lacking. Should one not be ashamed? The sage taught people not to overstep their rank; hence it is said, “Act according to your station.” Laozi said, “He who straddles does not walk.” Since you now have this will toward the Way, then from today on be careful and meticulous; go on working according to the rules. Take one true mind and go forward with what is before you, learning the Way without defilement. If you do not let the present moment pass at any time, then the future will not be empty. But if you use empty imagining and a mere promise in the present and wait for the future, that is to cross a river and seek a well to quench your thirst — is that not foolish? Let Tan Liangsheng look directly at the one point of not letting the present pass in vain, and he will see where his life comes to rest.
Instructions to Cao Shiju

In daily use the common people never depart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and the sage is the same. Their function being the same, yet there being the difference of sage and commoner, lies only in knowing and not knowing. Hence it is said, “The common people use it daily and do not know it.” The student’s work of restoring sagehood lies only at the place of not knowing in daily use, seeking the knowing that he originally possesses. If he sees the knowing that he originally has, then toward all sounds, forms, goods, and profit he is clear and not moved by them; meeting conditions and encountering circumstances thus, he is like a mirror showing reflections, and not a single thing can move within him. This is the essential gate of entering the Way.
Instructions to Feng Yanling

In turning toward the Way a student must first fear birth and death. Second, he must know the root of birth and death. The root of birth and death is precisely the various kinds of aversion, craving, taking, rejecting, self-pride, greed, hatred, and delusion that appear before him in daily use. Since these are the bitter root of birth and death, he must resolve to cut them off. There is no other technique: simply, when they arise, illuminate them at once and allow them no rise. At the place where they do not arise, they are dissolved right there. When they are dissolved, do not let them continue. Applying the mind thus, not letting a single thought pass at any time, mind after mind undimmed, one’s knowing becomes numinous of itself. If the knowing is numinous, then when it touches objects the objects do not drag the mind, and when it contemplates the mind the mind does not adhere to objects. With mind and objects not reaching each other, birth and death have no place to lodge. Applying the mind thus, there is no need to seek the mysterious and wondrous elsewhere.
Instructions to the Novice Hanhui Qi on Dwelling in the Mountains (Bingchen Year)

Qi first paid homage to Master Daguan and sought the Dharma of transcending the world. The Master approved and sent him to consult the Elder, who had him ordained and dyed. He relied on the Elder for several years; then, for the sake of the work of carving the great canon, he returned to serve his original teacher. That great task was not a matter of one day. Now, in old age and illness, he sought a place of great rest, and his plan had come to nothing. When the Elder came to Shuangjing and saw Qi, his spirit was weak but his mind’s strength was stronger; for more than ten years he had gained the single road that goes upward and had a little grip on it, lacking only that one shout of sudden breakthrough. When they spoke of a place to retire, the Elder taught him, saying: The whole great earth is a place of stillness and cessation; it lies only in the place where a student is willing to put things down, and that is the place of rest. Why seek it elsewhere? The ancient worthy said, “Not apart from true suchness is the place of standing; the place of standing is itself true.” It is only because one’s own mind arises and ceases and one follows feeling in all kinds of taking and rejecting that everywhere there are obstructions. The Third Patriarch said: “The ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes picking and choosing.” He also said, “It is because of taking and rejecting that it is not so.” If it is not so, then throughout the ten directions there is no place of rest. The Elder observes that Shuangjing is the place where the eighty-eight Patriarchs taught the Dharma, and where Chan Master Dahui also came to rest. Even your own original teacher, whose heels covered the seas, had no place to plant his foot; in the end, because of the work of carving the great canon, his bones were buried in the same pit as Dahui’s. How much more you, who followed your teacher’s wheel of vow and carved the scriptures at Jizhao’s founding — these are all places where you spent your life, and are the place where you may give up body and life. The Elder knows that what you cannot give up is not laziness but the fact that the view of self is not forgotten. In the pure dharma-realm, Buddhas, Patriarchs, and living beings all have a share; only the one with the view of self cannot enter. If one sees that there is a self, then one looks on Buddhas and Patriarchs as human forms; human forms stand opposed to me, and thus in the end there is no person to be avoided and no place to rest. If you yourself do not rest, then there is no place to rest; if you are willing to rest, then you rest on the spot. Putting everything down is the great rest. When you rest, Buddhas and living beings alike hide their shadows, and there is no place to contain them. You seek the road that goes upward; though it is called extraordinary, it is not as good as putting it down and being level and at peace. The ancients said, “When the household and the land are level and at peace, people are few.” If you reach the ground of levelness and peace, then even a Buddha is not made — what further upward is there to seek?
Instructions to the Chan Monk Shijing Yi

Because the ancients had not clearly understood the great matter of birth and death, they went into the mountains and dwelt alone in solitude, hanging their shadows there, solely to investigate clearly the matter beneath their own feet. Hence it is said, “While the great matter is not yet clear, one is as though bereaved of father and mother.” It is not to nurse laziness and seek idleness and pass the time as one pleases. If you truly want to investigate this great matter, you may only carry dung out, never carry dung in. You must spit out deluded thoughts and bad habits and the knowing and seeing of letters all at once, and let your breast be clean and gone, not a single dharma standing before the mind, with only one huatou as your own root of life. The ancients’ thirty years of not mixing the mind is precisely this. But if you now dwell in the mountains and drift idly as you please, giving free rein to feeling, and when a deluded thought arises you must patch together a few lines of poetry and compose a couple of verses, taking them as the principle of awakening to pass the days — then you are only a lazy fool nursing idleness. How can you be called a person of the Way dwelling in the mountains? You not only waste the light of time but consume in vain the offerings of the faithful. When you come to the last day of the twelfth month, with what will you face Old Man Yama? You cannot get past him with a poem and a verse. The Chan monk should think about why he dwells in the mountains: in the end he must find a landing place, and only then will he not betray the excellent affinity of one meeting through a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives. The ancient worthy said: “Those who suffer in the hells of the three paths are not truly suffering; to lose the human body beneath the robe — that is truly suffering.” Can one not keep this in mind?
The Dream Wanderings Collection of Elder Hanshan, Volume Seven
Instructions to the Chan Monk Taisu Yuan

When a student has first studied the teachings and then turns his mind to the road that goes upward, though he has the will, there is no help for the fact that in his storehouse consciousness there are the newly perfumed habits of the mixed poison of letters, and the old habits of greed, hatred, delusion, craving, and affliction; inner and outer attack each other, and it is hardest of all to pack away. What he wants to put down he cannot put down; what he wants to cut off he cannot cut off; what he wants to stop he cannot stop. Therefore he must raise a huatou; but it is like a gourd on the water — he cannot press it under, and can only wrestle with it, and it is the hardest thing to take in hand. And when he cannot take it in hand, he beats the retreat drum. Such a one is a person without aspiration and without strength — what is the use of talking about Chan investigation to him? Beginners today should simply put down at once all the principles and knowing and seeing within and without the mind, along with deluded thoughts and imaginings — put down and put down again, until there is nowhere left to put down; and only then raise one public case as a huatou, such as Zhaozhou’s word “No,” laid across the breast. Why did he say “No”? Bring down the doubt again. If the doubt has power, deluded thoughts will not arise. If you see them just beginning to arise, on no account set yourself against them and try to cut them off with the mind; nor may you use the mind to stop them, nor may you continue them. Simply see them, and let them go; with one letting go they dissolve. Quickly raise the huatou and look deeply into it, and those deluded thoughts will naturally vanish without trace. This is the formula for a beginner taking the work in hand. When the huatou is pure and familiar, deluded thoughts will naturally be rare and will not become obstructions. After a long time, when the doubt has power and deluded thoughts are temporarily at rest, you will gain a single moment of joy. But do not take that joy as something extraordinary; from there simply work well. The Chan monk abandons the teachings for Chan; for a beginner this is the hardest thing. Therefore I teach him this. On no account regard it as a small matter.
Instructions to the Chan Monk Henghe Zhi on Holding the Lotus Sutra

The Chan monk left home at Fudu and long served Master Dan as an attendant, gaining the Dharma gate of endurance and maintenance. He dwelt at Huacheng for years; Huacheng is the place where the great canon was carved and a Dharma cave within the seas. The monk put his strength into the permanent dwelling and managed the hundred affairs. When the Elder came to Shuangjing, the monk bowed and asked for instruction, wishing to hold the Lotus Sutra. So the Elder instructed him, saying: For the sake of the one great matter and its causes and conditions the Buddha appeared in the world — that is, to open and show all living beings the Buddha’s knowing and seeing and cause them to awaken and enter. What is called the Buddha’s knowing and seeing is the Buddha-nature that living beings originally possess. Now it is sealed and covered by ignorance and has become deluded knowing and seeing; and so in daily seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing one follows feeling and creates karma, and so takes on the suffering of birth and death without knowing it. Our master Śākyamuni came into the world expressly once, solely to open and show this matter and cause people to awaken to what they originally possess, not seeking it outside. If one awakens to this original possession, then whatever functions in response to conditions at the gates of the six faculties in daily use is the Buddha-wisdom present before one, and is called the Buddha’s knowing and seeing, not the deluded knowing and seeing of living beings. If one awakens to this knowing and seeing, then everywhere and in every dharma there is true application of mind, and all movements and practices are true wondrous practice, all becoming the true cause of Buddhahood. Hence the scripture says: “Even raising a single hand, or giving a slight bow of the head, even one stick of incense or one flower offered to the Buddha — all have already accomplished the Buddha Way.” Slight causes and small good deeds all become the true cause of Buddhahood; how much more so to bear responsibility for the assembly’s affairs and give one’s life for the Dharma — is this not the true seed of Buddhahood? When our Buddha taught people to hold the Lotus Sutra, he meant entering the Tathāgata’s room, wearing the Tathāgata’s robe, and sitting on the Tathāgata’s seat. The Tathāgata’s room is the mind of great compassion; the Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and patience; the Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all dharmas. If the monk can honor these three teachings of the Tathāgata, he is truly one who holds the scripture. If he cannot enter these three Dharma gates, then let him simply hold the chapter on the Practice of Ease and Bliss, thinking of it thought after thought and wishing to enter it mind after mind, day and night without forgetting. Then the sixty thousand-odd words will be luminous word by word, appearing at the gates of the six faculties. If he does not enter this Dharma gate, then even if he can hold a hundred thousand myriad copies, he only makes an enemy of the meaning — is he truly one who holds the scripture? If you do not believe the Elder, then go and ask Mañjuśrī and Maitreya.
Instructions to Wang Lunian (Sixth Day of the New Year, Dingsi Year)

The student Wang Lunian grew up in Huaixi, came to pay homage at Mount Jing, and asked the Elder for a word. The Elder saw that he bore a righteous spirit and had a compassionate heart, and so said to him: Have you heard that in ancient times there were men of great strength? To conquer others is folly; to conquer oneself is wisdom. The fool is always weak; the wise are always victorious — this is the way of things. The sage taught people to use non-use as use; hence it is said, “The soft overcomes the hard; the weak overcomes the strong.” The Changes says, “Hard yet able to be soft — the way of good fortune.” Xiang Yu uprooted mountains and lifted cauldrons, his strength the mightiest of a thousand ages; but when he was defeated and parted from Consort Yu, he sobbed and shed several lines of tears. He could conquer others but could not conquer himself. The sage pointed this out directly to Yan Yuan: “To overcome oneself and return to propriety is benevolence.” Students past and present all know the words “overcome oneself,” but cannot do the work of conquering themselves — how is that wisdom? If Wang Lunian has strength in this, he should not fall among the ranks of ordinary men.
Instructions to the Attendant Zaiyong

The attendant Yong was born in Western Shu and in his youth was sunk in mean service. Fortunately his prajñā-cause was not obscured, and while still young he knew to consult Master Miaofeng and roused the mind to leave the world — surely the inward perfuming of seeds planted long ago made him so. It happened that Master Danju entered Shu, and at that time Yong was serving Mr. Xu. The latter had always admired his faith, and so ordered him to pay homage to Master Dan and seek the Dharma of escaping suffering, and he was tonsured as a novice. When the Elder came to Shuangjing, Yong served as his attendant, diligent day and night without slackness. The Elder at first pitied his dullness and constantly roused him; whenever Yong heard the Elder instruct the patch-robed monks, his brows would stir with animation. Know then that the seed of Buddha-nature in living beings waits for its time to sprout. When he asked for instruction, the Elder taught him the public case of examining who it is that recites the Buddha’s name and told him to investigate it. Yong could also receive and bear it. I fear only that he lacks the decided mind for birth and death and cannot risk his life to the very end; and I fear too that bad habits and bad knowing and seeing may obstruct him midway and carry him into the net of false views. Apart from these two faults, then with the single thought, tightly embracing the mass of doubt through the six periods of day and night, even twenty or thirty years without awakening he should not rest. Even if he does not awaken in this life, it will become a surpassing cause, and in a future life when he gets out he will know this matter; though many kalpas pass, he will never lose the seed of the right cause. But if his resolve is not firm and his application not keen, and he gives rise to false thoughts instead, then he will not only betray this life — through a thousand lives and ten thousand kalpas there will be no share in getting out.
Instructions to the Attendant Zaijie

Elder Zibo bore the great Dharma wholly on his body and wished to establish the enterprise of reviving the Dharma gate; therefore he devoted his strength to printing the great canon. This one great matter and its causes and conditions was no small thing. In the end he entrusted the whole burden to Master Dan to carry on one shoulder. Since the canon was carved but could not be stored in a fitting place, the work of restoring Huacheng was again no small thing. And Huacheng’s restoration was not the work of one hand or one foot. The attendant Jie took the lead with courage in every matter, not avoiding hardship or danger, and his merit was the greater part. This again was the hardest thing among the many. It has been said that in the world there is no one who gladly uses his strength for nothing — even the heroes of old were so, how much more others? When Emperor Gaozu of Han had settled the empire and the meritorious officials were not yet enfeoffed, he suddenly saw them whispering in the sand. He asked Zhang Zifang. Zifang said: “These are men who braved arrows and stones amid weapons and passed through ten thousand deaths and one life; all of them want a fief of a few feet. Now that they have not seen any enfeoffment, they are whispering.” Thereupon he enfeoffed them at once. This was the old rule for employing people. Now consider the attendant Jie: at first he had no other aim but to leave home. Now he has run about for seven years, and Huacheng is settled; the great Dharma has found its place. Among those who take credit for the work, would there be none who whisper? The Elder says that now one may reward him with the Tathāgata’s reward. The attendant Jie has, through the Elder, received the Tathāgata’s great reward. But if he cannot honor the Tathāgata’s Dharma, keep the Tathāgata’s precepts, and do the Tathāgata’s work, and if by any chance he breaks the precepts and destroys the Dharma, the Tathāgata too has his three-foot blade. Be careful!
